thoughts.t: One should know that the true meaning of satsang is to associate with the ātmā, which is true; to associate with Paramatma, who is true; to associate with the guru, who is true; and to associate with true shastras. One who practises this divine satsang becomes blissful.
Bhagwan is the all-doer, compassionate and the protector of all; at all times, he alone is the resolver of all my adversities.
Whatever Bhagwan does is always beneficial. His wish alone is my prārabdh. He alone is my liberator.
My hindrances, sins, flaws and bad qualities will certainly be destroyed. I will surely attain peace, supreme bliss and happiness.
This is because I have attained the manifest form of Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj. With his strength, I will surely overcome misery.
With the strength of such thoughts, a devotee who has taken refuge never loses courage and remains joyous due to the strength of Bhagwan.
One should respectfully associate with a person who has firm devotion and conviction in Akshar-Purushottam and who is discerning.
One should respectfully associate with those who do not doubt the words of Bhagwan or the guru, and are trustworthy and wise.
One should respectfully associate with those who always eagerly follow commands with enthusiasm and determination, and are humble and cooperative.
One should respectfully associate with those who lovingly see divinity in both the divine and human-like actions of Bhagwan and the guru.
One should respectfully associate with those in satsang who eagerly imbibe the virtues of others, never speak about others' flaws and keep suhradbhāv.
One should respectfully associate with a person whose conduct and thoughts aim solely to please the guru.
One should study and teach the Sanskrit or vernacular texts of one's Sampraday according to one's abilities and preferences.
When we control our attitude and response to the events and circumstances that unfold in our lives, we gain a level of control over our life itself.
In happiness, do not get carried away. In misery, do not become discouraged.

The body and mind are considered the 'pseudo-self,' while the soul is the 'real self.'... Mind is closely related to the immune system, and a disturbed or weak mind can lead to illness. Building the mind through spiritual practices like satsang is comparable to building the body at a gym.
When we learn to bow down with respect and let go of unnecessary ego, life becomes more peaceful and joyful.

Spiritual understanding (samjan) is the root answer. Then, all questions will be solved... Doing things out of understanding will sustain your spirituality, whereas other (worldly) things will come and go, stay or disappear.

Prapti is like the great and big Himalayas, while our worldly problems are like small heaps of mud. Our focus should always be on our prapti. Our worldly problems are petty, temporary, and limited to this life.

teachings.title: Prapti: the train to Delhi
parts: Mahant Swami Maharaj explains the idea of prapti by saying that it is as big as the Himalayas, while our worldly problems are like small heaps of mud. Our focus should always be on our prapti. Our worldly problems are petty, temporary and limited to this life. On the other hand, realizing prapti results in a permanent relief and liberation from the cycle of births and deaths.

Mahant Swami Maharaj illustrates this further by saying that suppose you are successfully running a big factory in Ahmedabad. Then, due to a new official regulation your factory operations stall. The matter becomes more complicated, resulting into legal issues with some higher officials in New Delhi.

Despite your best of efforts in meeting the officials in Delhi, the matter remains unresolved. You return home to Gujarat, desperate to resolve the ongoing heavy losses in capital, production and market share. Now, suddenly out of the blue, you get a call from the authorities in Delhi asking you to urgently meet them the next day at 11 a.m.

To get there, no air or train reservation ticket is available. But, you manage to get into a train without any reservation for a bunk to sleep or a seat. Consequently, you reach Delhi the next morning, standing all the way. You are extremely tired and exhausted when you reach your meeting place at 11 a.m.

At 11.15 a.m., your file is cleared by the concerned official, giving you permission to recommence your factory operations. Consequently, you are greatly relieved. In this situation, will you remember or feel the pain and struggle of your train journey?
The answer is no, because a bigger problem has been solved for which you had been struggling and making efforts for quite some time.

Then, Swamishri explains that souls have been struggling for countless births to obtain moksha. It is only in this life that we have come in the contact of the Satpurush and satsang to enable us to solve our long struggle to achieve permanent relief and happiness.

If we keep this in mind, then the problems of this world are trifle, like the difficulties of the train journey to Delhi. This is how Swamishri explains in very simple terms the concept of spiritual prapti in this life and why we should rejoice and always remain joyous.
teachings.take: The biggest thing is already solved: I have met the Satpurush. Today's struggle is the train journey.
teachings.reflect: What is my 'train journey' right now?
teachings.src: Uniqueness of Mahant Swami Maharaj's Speech (Part 1)
reflects: What is my 'train journey' right now?
If my prapti is the Himalayas, what is today's heap of mud?
What is one discomfort I can put up with today, knowing where I'm going?
When did a problem feel huge and then turn out small?
What does it feel like to know my 'file' has already been cleared?
Which worry could I set next to my prapti for a moment and compare?
What would I tell a friend standing all night on their own train?
What small thing today reminds me that I have met the Satpurush?
What can I do today that the tired, standing me would be proud of?
Where have Maharaj & Swami already carried me through something hard?

teachings.title: The bucket and the ocean
parts: "Even great avatars and devotees of the past have gone through pain," he explained. "Even Dada Khachar, who gave everything to Bhagwan Swaminarayan and received his blessings numerous times that 'all will be well', went through failure after failure, downturn after downturn. But they never lost faith. They carried on.

"If you carry a bucket of water on your head, how much weight will you experience? It will feel heavy. But if you dive into the ocean and thousands of tons of water pass over your head, do you feel its weight? No. Similarly, do not carry such burden on your head. Leave it to God. Immerse yourself in his devotion. He is the all-doer. You will never feel burdened."
teachings.take: Carried alone, it's a heavy bucket. Given to Maharaj, it's the ocean.
teachings.reflect: What am I carrying on my head that I can hand over today?
teachings.src: A Chill Pill for Mental Wellness

Dada Khachar kept going. What is one small way I can keep going today?

What could I put down for ten minutes today?

teachings.title: Body and soul
parts: Explaining the concept of body and soul, Mahant Swami Maharaj gives the following analogy. Suppose that someone enacts the role of King Alexander the Great in a drama. To make the character realistic, the actor displays all the characteristics of King Alexander. However, he himself is fully aware that he is just playing a role of Alexander and that he is not the king.

Similarly, Swamishri says that in reality we are atma. However, as human beings we have to discharge our duties as a father or mother, brother or sister, son or daughter. Like the actor staging the drama knows he isn't Alexander the Great, we must also be very clear that we are atma and different from the body and merely playing a role only.
We must try to remember this in all stages of our life.
teachings.take: I am atma, playing a role. The role is not who I am.
teachings.reflect: Which role feels heavy today? Can I play it while remembering I am atma?
teachings.src: Uniqueness of Mahant Swami Maharaj's Speech (Part 1)
reflects: Which role feels heavy today? Can I play it while remembering I am atma?
What role am I playing today that isn't the whole of me?
If today's feeling is a costume, what's underneath it?
Which part of my day could I act out calmly, like the actor who knows?
What would the atma in me notice about today?
Which label have I been wearing too tightly?
What stays the same in me on good days and hard days?
Who do I become when I remember I'm not just my thoughts?
What is one role I'm grateful to be playing right now?
How can I be kind to the actor, even when the scene is hard?

teachings.title: Purpose of human life
parts: Mahant Swami Maharaj explains that suppose you are a businessman and you are on a business trip to London for a week. During your stay in London, will you take your meals or not? Of course. But did you specifically go to London to take meals? The answer is no. Then, during your stay there for a week, will you sleep or not? Of course, you will. But did you go to London to sleep?

No. Similarly, as a human we must fulfil our worldly duties and interests of earning a livelihood, family responsibilities, social commitments, recreation, etc. However, these aren't the main reasons for our human birth. The main purpose of attaining moksha for one's soul should never be forgotten.
teachings.take: Work, family and daily life matter, but they aren't why we are here.
teachings.reflect: What is one worldly worry today that I can hold a little more lightly?
teachings.src: Uniqueness of Mahant Swami Maharaj's Speech (Part 1)

What is one thing I did today just for satsang?
If this week were a business trip, what's the real business?
What can I let be 'just a meal' today, not the whole trip?
Where did I notice my purpose today, even briefly?
What would I like my days to be about a year from now?

teachings.title: On anger
parts: Mahant Swami Maharaj explains that people often get angry on someone over small matters. There may be times, depending on the circumstances, when one has to tell someone off. Swamishri says the important thing is how much to tell, how to tell and when to tell. Then, he elaborates it with an example. To heat 100ml of water, would it make sense to burn 1 metric ton of coal?

Similarly, there are times when too much anger is not warranted. Sometimes, one faces minor issues and so saying a little may suffice. But, at times we get extremely angry, which then spoils the matter further, including our health, peace of mind and spirituality. Thus, Swamishri teaches the need to control one's anger.
teachings.take: Match the response to the size of the matter: don't burn a ton of coal for 100ml of water.
teachings.reflect: Is this 100ml or a ton?
teachings.src: Uniqueness of Mahant Swami Maharaj's Speech (Part 1)
reflects: Is this 100ml or a ton?

What usually sits underneath my irritation: tiredness, worry or hurt?

When did I handle something calmly that I'm proud of?
What is one small thing I could let pass today?

teachings.title: On happiness
parts: Mahant Swami Maharaj explains the concept of happiness by posing a question: If you can sleep peacefully for eight hours on a bed worth ₹5,000, then for how many hours can you sleep on a bed costing ₹50,000? And what if the bed is worth ₹500,000, ₹5,000,000 or ₹50,000,000? Swamishri replies that happiness does not increase in proportion to having greater wealth or more expensive things. Wealth can provide convenience, but not inner peace, which is a totally different domain.
teachings.take: Comfort is not the same as peace.
teachings.reflect: What gave me peace today that cost nothing?
teachings.src: Uniqueness of Mahant Swami Maharaj's Speech (Part 1)

teachings.title: Body, mind and soul: the three partners
parts: Mahant Swami Maharaj explains the difference between deha (body), man (mind) and atma (soul) in the following way. He says that in business, there is generally a working partner, managing partner and a financing partner. The financing partner is most critical for starting and running the business.

Similarly, Swamishri compares that in life the body is a working partner, the mind is a managing partner and the atma is a financing partner – the most important player. However, in business the working partner often takes the maximum share of the profit, followed by the managing partner and the financing partner gets the least.

Similarly, in life, people spend most of their time on their body and mind and very little for their atma. The essence of Mahant Swami Maharaj's analogy is that we should prioritize and focus our efforts and resources in elevating our atma to attain moksha.
teachings.take: The atma is the partner that matters most, and usually gets the least time.
teachings.reflect: What is one small thing I can give my atma today?
teachings.src: Uniqueness of Mahant Swami Maharaj's Speech (Part 2)
reflects: What is one small thing I can give my atma today?

What is one habit that looks after all three partners?
When did my atma feel strongest this month?
What would a good day for all three partners look like?
Where have I been running on empty?

teachings.title: Traffic jam or swabhav jam?
parts: Mahant Swami Maharaj often speaks about a big traffic congestion which he had once encountered. All the vehicles had come to a standstill. On investigating, it was found that there was a problem between two vehicles on a narrow section of the road, where neither driver was willing to give way to each other.

Mahant Swami Maharaj explains that it wasn't a traffic jam, but a swabhav (temperament) jam. If one of the drivers had reversed a little, the congestion would have eased totally. However, because of their egos, neither were willing to take a step back. Swamishri emphasizes that in life, too, we face such problems. In most cases they are a result of our swabhavs.
teachings.take: Reversing a little clears the road.
teachings.reflect: Where could I take one step back today?
teachings.src: Uniqueness of Mahant Swami Maharaj's Speech (Part 2)

teachings.title: The first rocket
parts: Abdul Kalam, in his book, Transcendence, describes to Pramukh Swami Maharaj, "Swamiji, when I first launched a rocket it failed, and I became very depressed and disheartened. At the time I thought of becoming a sannyasi and giving up everything."

Pramukh Swami Maharaj said, "The Bhagavad Gita defines renunciation in a unique way, 'One must renounce not the performance of deeds, but renounce the desire for the fruits of those actions.'… Human effort and God's grace move this world. Even failure of the first rocket, which you faced, was for your good; it prodded you to make things better."
teachings.take: A setback isn't the end of the story. Effort is mine, grace is His.
teachings.reflect: What did my last setback teach me?

teachings.title: The bumble-bee
parts:
Swami-Shreeji
P.P. Pramukh Swami
Swami Bapa's most blessed Bal-Muktos
Heartiest Jai Shree Swaminarayan from Sadhu Keshavjivandas.
According to science, a bumble-bee with its weight and small delicate wings should not fly. But it does. Why? Because it thinks it can. So, you also can do, whatever you desire. So, everybody say, I CAN, I WILL, I MUST (C W M). Many can but they don't will. We belong to Swami Bapa. We should become HIS PRIDE. And, therefore we MUST.

Swami Bapa's blessings are there to excel in studies. Do the best. Everyone will have grand success in your final exams. Pray and put your best efforts.
Jai Swaminarayan.
teachings.take: The bumble-bee flies because it thinks it can. I belong to Swami Bapa.

teachings.title: I am atma, servant of Purushottam
parts: Discoursing after puja, Swamishri said, “Maharaj manifested on earth to teach us that the body and atma are separate. So do not waste this life and opportunity. We have attained this birth and God’s manifest association. This is a great opportunity, so do not waste it. Believe ‘I am the atma, not the body’ and live accordingly. Strengthen this belief daily. We say ‘Aksharam aham, Purushottam dāsosmi,’ but we must live it day and night – 24 hours. Throughout the day, frequently repeat, ‘I am akshar, but am the servant of Purushottam’. This is the focus of our sadhana.”

After his puja , Swamishri discoursed, “The body and atma are separate. By assuming yourself to be the body, you experience misery. Believe your true form to be atma and there will be no miseries. So, all the pain everybody experiences is due to body-consciousness. We have attained this satsang, the Satpurush and Bhagwan. But problems remain due to one’s body-centredness. If this is overcome, one will experience unbroken joy. Remaining attached to the body leads to great deficiencies.”

After puja, Swamishri blessed, “Over countless births, the body and atma have become one. But they are distinct. Understanding this is the goal of satsang. It is not possible to physically separate the two, but it must be done through understanding. With such wisdom, one lives in the body, but knows the atma to be separate.”
teachings.take: Much of the heaviness comes from believing I am only the body. I am atma, the servant of Purushottam.
teachings.reflect: When today feels heavy, what could I say to myself instead of “I am this feeling”?
reflects: When today feels heavy, what could I say to myself instead of 'I am this feeling'?
What does 'Aksharam aham' mean to me today?
How could I live one hour today as atma, not body?
What feeling have I mistaken for who I am?
What is one way to strengthen this belief daily?
When did I feel like a servant of Purushottam?
What would I do differently today if I truly believed I am atma?
Which thought today could I watch pass, rather than become?
What opportunity have I been given that I don't want to waste?
What small seva could I offer today?

teachings.title: When you have God, you have everything
parts: In 1988, Pramukh Swami Maharaj was in Los Angeles. An American by the name of Carlos Vegas met Swamishri. He was depressed so he asked for Swamishri’s prayer and blessings. He said, “I have everything in life. I have a nice big house and a car. I have a wife and kids. I have money…”
Swamishri stopped him, “Listen, I don’t have money. But I have God. When you have God, you have everything.”
teachings.take: Whatever I lack right now, I have God. That is everything.

teachings.title: The biggest prize
parts: Once, Swamishri was in Birmingham. While on the way to his residence, someone said, “It is Dr Swami’s wish that you be awarded with the Nobel Peace Prize. The award-giving ceremony takes place in Stockholm, Sweden. This award should be given to you in the presence of sadhus and thousands of devotees.”

Swamishri immediately responded, “For us, the biggest prize is having met Shastriji Maharaj and Yogiji Maharaj. Everything is included in them. They are the topmost of the top. (Nobel na pan Nobel chhe). That Maharaj and Swami are happy and Shastriji Maharaj and Yogiji Maharaj have blessed us is the greatest of all prizes.”

Aksharjivandas Swami, one of the swamis who was on that vicharan tour, politely asked Swamishri, “Can you please write a few words of blessings in my notebook? It will be a memory that I can treasure.”

Swamishri took the notebook and put it aside. Then, he said, “Listen, I have never felt like asking Shastriji Maharaj or Yogiji Maharaj for their blessings in writing. Nor have I ever longed for some relic of theirs, such as a rosary, a fingernail, a strand of hair, or a piece of cloth. I have never desired for such mementos. However, I have focused on one thing: to follow their commands no matter what. I have done that right from the beginning, ever since I came into Satsang. Today, I feel fulfilled having followed their every wish and every word. That has been the goal of my life. As a result, I constantly feel their rajipo. Shastriji Maharaj and Yogiji Maharaj are always with me.”
teachings.take: Having met the guru is the greatest prize. Following his words keeps him with me.

teachings.title: With you forever
parts: At some points in our lives we go through some form of stress, and during those times it feels like we’re being hemmed in by it. It’s as if we can only be at peace if the source of stress vanishes. When one searches for any remedies to stress or anxiety, some of them may work, but they do not provide a long-term fix. For example, say your personal treatment for stress is spending time with friends and family. What if something changed in the dynamics of your friends or family; this meant you couldn’t spend as much time with them as you would like. We have all heard the popular saying, “Friends come and go, but family is with you forever.” This can be extended to include a third dimension: Friends may come and go; family may also come and go, but Shriji Maharaj and the Satpurush are with you forever.

In the Satsang Diksha, Mahant Swami Maharaj writes, “Bhagwan je kare te sadāy sārā māte hoy. Temni ichchhā e ja māru prārabdha chhe. Teo ja mārā tārak chhe.” This translates to, “Whatever Bhagwan does is always beneficial. His wish alone is my prarabdha. He alone is my liberator.” Although success in our world is important, it should not override our aim to achieve moksha. Bhagwan will do what he wills. Our priority should be to attain moksha and when we physically depart from this earth our atmas enter Akshardham. With this thought, stress won’t enter our minds and through this mindset, our lives will become much happier.

Rather than thinking that we have got this human body to get a good job and earn lots of money, we should think that we are primarily here to attain Akshardham and not materialistic things. You have probably read that line or something very similar a thousand times and are probably thinking to yourself, “I get it!” True, it is easier said than done, so why not start to think like this in small steps. Any time we get stressed or nervous or overwhelmed, we should think to ourselves, “I am atma and not the body.” The main purpose of our life is to follow niyams and attain moksha. Essentially, detach yourself from worldly activities and attach yourself to Bhagwan. Keep your worldly life modest and your satsang above all else. Strive to earn a successful living but whenever you feel life is too much, don’t become absorbed in that journey, but rather become absorbed in your efforts to attain Akshardham. By doing this and changing your mindset, stress will slowly disintegrate.
teachings.take: People and plans change. Shriji Maharaj and the Satpurush stay with me forever.

teachings.title: Flexibility is the key to stability
parts: Once, Pramukh Swami Maharaj was in Bochasan, Gujarat. A young devotee had just bought a new set of Flexon eyeglasses. He explained, “Swamishri, these glasses cost 18,000 rupees. They are more durable and resistant than conventional metals, allowing them to be flexed, bent, or twisted and still they return to their original shape.” He then took off his glasses and bent the frame, but it did not break. Swamishri smiled and said, “If we are flexible in life, we can adjust to any situation. Accordingly, we become stable, and our value increases.” Flexibility is the key to stability. Problems, difficulties and hardships disappear when we are willing to become flexible.

Following his 59th birthday celebration in 1979, Rajkot, Swamishri was visiting the homes of well-wishers and devotees in the city. Suddenly, his car ran out of fuel and came to a halt. The driver requested Swamishri to remain seated in the car while he looked for a petrol station. But Swamishri told him, “If we wait around, we’ll be late for the next town which is at least two hours’ drive from here.” He got out of the car in an instant and took a three-wheeler public rickshaw to continue with the rest of the home visits. It was nothing new for him to travel that way, because earlier in his life there were no special travel arrangements for him. Sometimes, he travelled in a bullock cart or in a wagon attached to a tractor. But his main mode of transport was either a State Transport bus or a third-class compartment on a local train. Even as the President of BAPS, no special provisions or privileges were ever afforded to him. Often, he slept on wooden benches or under a neem tree. Sometimes, he even slept on a heap of sand. He had no specific office or workplace; wherever he worked became his workplace. Amazingly, Swamishri never complained about anything or made a fuss. For him, serving humanity was of paramount importance, with or without special arrangements.
teachings.take: Bending with a situation is not breaking. It is how I stay steady.

teachings.title: No shoes, no feet
parts: Pramukh Swami Maharaj gave a wonderful illustration in his discourses about why we should never compare ourselves with others when it comes to material possessions. A poor boy was begging on the streets of a busy city. He dreamt of wearing a nice pair of shoes and thought to himself that one day he would have enough money to buy a pair. Once, as he was looking at everyone’s shoes, he saw a big car pull over on the other side of the road. The driver stepped down and got a wheelchair out from the back. Next, he opened the back seat door and helped a man on to the wheelchair. The boy’s eyes were fixed on the nicely dressed man seated in the wheelchair. But he noticed that the man had no feet. He only had legs that were cut off from the knee down. The little boy thought to himself, “I was sad because I had no shoes until I saw a man who had no feet.”

It dawned upon the boy that happiness or sadness is not a matter of worldly possessions or good fortune. It is a matter of attitude. One can be fully satisfied and happy sleeping under a tree but miserable and stressed out in an air-conditioned room. It is all in the mind.
teachings.take: Comparing steals my peace. Contentment is an attitude I can practise.

teachings.title: Questions for Pramukh Swami Maharaj
parts:
Q: What should we do when we face insurmountable miseries and difficulties in life?
Swamishri: Associating with the Gunatit Sant will give you peace. He will help you to overcome them.

Q. The Satpurush is omniscient (antaryami). So why is it necessary to confess one’s mistakes to him?
Swamishri: The Satpurush is all-knowing, but Shastriji Maharaj and Yogiji Maharaj used to say, “Tell the antaryami seven times.” We know him as omniscient, but a barrier remains. By confessing, that barrier is removed and one experiences inner peace and joy.

Q. When someone lapses in observing the five vartmans, what can we do to avoid taking abhav-avgun? Do satsangis have a responsibility in that?
Swamishri: Do not harass one who lapses in observing the five vartmans. If one has a rapport with them then one can tell them, otherwise do not keep their company. Do not spread any talks about their misdeeds. Bhagwan will give them the appropriate fruits of their actions. We are not responsible for them. Everybody is liable to make mistakes.
We are here [in satsang] to become pure. If you focus on this, there will be no problems.

Q: What is the future like for this world?
PSM: It is in the hands of God. The future depends on our faith in God. There will always be ups and downs. But God showers compassion on humans and will continue to do so.
teachings.take: Ups and downs will come. The Gunatit Sant helps me through them, and opening my heart brings peace.

teachings.title: With Bapa’s strength
parts: Pramukh Swami Maharaj read and replied to over 700,000 letters, devoting an average of two hours a day to counsel and console through his pen. And this he accomplished in the midst of constant travelling, attending assemblies, meeting devotees, attending administrative meetings and all his other activities.

In 1977, Swamishri wrote a letter from abroad during his hectic Satsang tour which sums up the situation nicely: “There is no end to our travelling and no end to the mail I have to deal with at all times in the car, when sitting or even in bed. Only then am I able to manage. But with (Yogi) Bapa’s strength, I am able to cope.”

Once, C.M. Patel of London gave a friendly comment to Swamishri in Bhadra, “Bapa! You keep writing letters all day. These sadhus don’t let you stay free for even one minute!”
Swamishri spoke, “This is our service to Maharaj.”

Today, Mahant Swami Maharaj remains equipoised and absorbed in divinity in all his daily activities. He gives his fullest attention to whatever he does: morning puja, Thakorji’s darshan, meeting the devotees and attending to letters. Thus, by having his darshan one becomes destressed and experiences inner tranquility.
teachings.take: I don’t have to cope on my own strength. I can cope with Bapa’s strength.

teachings.title: Not an iota of difference
parts: In 1988, devotees had taken Pramukh Swami Maharaj on a day trip to the Catalina Islands, off the coast of California. On the boat ride back, the swamis were singing godi and were enthralled by Swamishri’s swaying to the rhythm. C.M. Kaka, a senior devotee of London, noticed this and tapped Swamishri on the shoulder to enquire, “Swami, what are these swamis staring at?”

Gently, Swamishri leaned over and replied, “They are experiencing the happiness of Akshardham from me.”
“But Swami, I can’t experience it,” C.M. Kaka admitted.
Swamishri unhesitatingly remarked, “C.M., in the murti that resides in Akshardham, and the murti seated before you now – there is not an iota of difference; they are the same.”
Overjoyed by Swamishri’s unprompted revelation, C.M. Kaka, too, became engrossed in the divinity.

teachings.title: His wish prevails
parts: In 1974, Swamishri and his sadhus were given a grand farewell in Mumbai before they departed by flight to Nairobi. However, on landing at the airport in Nairobi they were ordered to return to Mumbai. The sadhus asked Swamishri, “Why has this happened?” He replied, “We have done no wrong. We do things to please Maharaj. So, his wish prevails.” It is clear from his answer how much at ease he was. A similar incident happened: the planning permission for a mandir in Harrow, London, was refused. The youths and devotees had tried very hard. The youths were confidently saying that they would get permission to construct the mandir, but they lost the case. Subsequently, everyone was disappointed. But that night Swamishri slept soundly. It was evident from this that he had no desire other than to please Maharaj and Swami. No pillow is as soft as a clear conscience. He had a pure heart.
teachings.take: When things don’t go to plan, I can still rest. I did my part; his wish prevails.

teachings.title: The boy who found his own classmates
parts: As a boy in Chansad, Shantilal (the future Pramukh Swami Maharaj) hit a wall. The village school stopped at the fifth standard, and no higher class could start without enough pupils. A teacher in nearby Darapara agreed to begin a class if ten students enrolled, so Shantilal went from village to village looking for them. He found about a dozen. Even then, the teacher lost interest and the class never began.

He spent that year at home, reading, going to the mandir and doing odd jobs, his wish to study as strong as ever. A school in Bochasan offered him a place, but only if he repeated two years he had already passed, so another year slipped by. At last he enrolled at the English school in Padra, six kilometres away. Two friends gave him lifts on their bicycles, and when he felt he was imposing, he simply walked.

Nothing about this was dramatic. It was a quiet young person being turned down, waiting, trying another door, and accepting help where it was offered. The setbacks did not tell him who he was. They were simply the road he happened to be on, and he kept putting one foot in front of the other until a way opened.
teachings.quote: His desire to study remained intense. He would not accept defeat.

teachings.title: And so things rolled on
parts: As a teenager, Shantilal was so quiet that when people spoke to him he often only managed a murmur in reply. Serving senior sadhus one holiday, he could not work out how to draw water from a well with a canvas bucket, and Ghanshyam Swami despaired of him. Another time he was sent to buy grapes for a herbal remedy and came back with fresh green ones instead of the dried black ones needed, and was scolded.

Balmukund Swami took him under his wing. Years later Pramukh Swami Maharaj remembered how that sadhu patiently showed him, again and again, how to wash dhotis (the plain cloth sadhus wear), scrub pots, cook and sing bhajans (devotional songs). Looking back on those awkward years, he never claimed to have been gifted. He said simply that his guru's blessings were with him, and so life carried on.

Decades later, when a devotee in Canada praised his skill as a manager, he answered in almost the same way: it was all Shastriji Maharaj's grace and Yogiji Maharaj's inspiration, and so things rolled on. The boy who could not manage a bucket went on to guide thousands. Being slow to learn, or unsure of yourself, is not the end of the story.

teachings.title: A fever and a promise
parts: Soon after leaving home to become a sadhu, Shantilal longed to see his guru, Shastriji Maharaj. Instead, the sadhu he was travelling with kept changing plans, and a journey of a few hours stretched into days. In Nadiad he came down with a fever. The others went out early each morning and came back late, so he lay alone on a makeshift bed for most of the day, weak and waiting.

When he finally reached Ahmedabad, still feverish, he was put to bed in a corner. Shastriji Maharaj came straight to him and said warmly that he was glad he had arrived at last. Shantilal could only manage to say that he had been unwell for a few days. His guru stroked his head and told him to rest. That night he returned, softly chanting 'Swaminarayan' and assuring him all would be well.

The fever broke that night. The next morning Shastriji Maharaj initiated him as a parshad, the first step towards becoming a sadhu. The lonely days in Nadiad had not been wasted. They ended beside someone who had been expecting him all along. When you feel alone and unwell, you are still being held, and still expected.

teachings.title: Saying what is on your heart
parts: Before he left home, Shantilal had been told he could study English. After his first initiation, Shastriji Maharaj suggested that Sanskrit would serve a sadhu better, since it would let him read the scriptures. Shantilal had already resolved to follow his guru's wishes. Even so, he told Shastriji Maharaj honestly that he had hoped to learn English. The book notes that this kind of open confession was something his guru welcomed.

Shastriji Maharaj did not simply give an order. He waited, and asked Harijivan Swami, a sadhu Shantilal was close to, to talk it over with him. One night in Gondal the two sat outside and talked until after half past one in the morning. At last Shantilal said he would study as his guru wished. Harijivan Swami woke Shastriji Maharaj with the news, and he was so delighted that he hugged Shantilal at once.

There is a quiet lesson here. Having hopes of your own is not disloyal, and saying them out loud is not a failing. A wise guide wants to know what is really in your heart. Good decisions are often reached slowly, in an unhurried conversation with someone who cares about you.

teachings.title: The President washed the plates
parts: In 1950 Shastriji Maharaj announced that the young sadhu Narayanswarupdas, still in his twenties, would become Pramukh (President) of BAPS. Some senior devotees worried he was too junior. Shastriji Maharaj replied that he had never regretted a decision, and that while they looked at the young man's body, he was looking at his soul. Narayanswarupdas himself felt others were better suited, and accepted only because he saw it was his guru's deepest wish.

The ceremony was held in a small, crowded room in Ahmedabad. Seated on a cot beside Shastriji Maharaj and Yogiji Maharaj, he felt embarrassed by the honour. When asked to speak, his words came out haltingly; he was never known as a speaker. Afterwards a meal was served to everyone. He wandered out into the yard, found a heap of dirty plates and pots under a tap, and sat down to wash them.

Pramukh Swami Maharaj never let a title change who he was. Being chosen did not make him feel above the smallest job, and feeling unready did not stop him saying yes. If you ever feel like an impostor in a new role, remember that the one who washed the plates was exactly the right person for it.

teachings.title: You serve me, so I serve you
parts: Pragat Bhagat was one of Pramukh Swami Maharaj's personal attendants. One morning, although a cut on his finger had become badly infected, he still went to fetch a pail of hot water for Swamishri's bath (Swamishri is the respectful name devotees use for him). In his hurry, he left his own unwashed dhoti, the plain cloth worn by sadhus and attendants, lying in the bathroom.

When he came back he was dismayed to find that Pramukh Swami Maharaj had washed and wrung out the dhoti for him. All Pragat Bhagat could do was ask why. The reply was simple and warm: since Pragat Bhagat served him in so many ways, he should serve Pragat Bhagat too. Many years later, the attendant still remembered that morning.

In the same chapter, Swamishri is found quietly cleaning the sadhus' toilets after a festival while others rested, and he cheerfully told the sadhu who tried to stop him to go and fetch water instead. For him, seva (selfless service) never flowed only upwards to the guru. It flowed back down too, to whoever was tired, hurt or overlooked.

What would change if kindness flowed both ways in all your relationships?
teachings.reflect: Who looks after you without being asked?

teachings.title: Thanking the man who hated sadhus
parts: In the village of Sokhda, a devotee named Purushottamdas wanted to host Yogiji Maharaj. The village chief, Jashbhai, despised sadhus. After days of pleading he grudgingly lent his house, the best in the village, but said he would stay elsewhere, would not come for darshan (a respectful audience with a holy person), and expected tobacco stains to be scrubbed off his walls. Purushottamdas tried to explain that these sadhus used no tobacco at all.

Yogiji Maharaj was unwell and sent Pramukh Swami Maharaj in his place. After two days, as he was about to leave, Swamishri asked whose house it was and wanted the owner called. Purushottamdas warned that Jashbhai hated sadhus and would only insult him by staying away. Swamishri gently pointed out that since they had stayed in the man's house, surely they owed him their thanks.

Jashbhai arrived fuming, with a few friends. On seeing Swamishri he fell at his feet and begged him to stay two more days, and Swamishri unpacked. Jashbhai's life changed: he began daily puja (personal worship) and later served in the mandir for the rest of his life. It all began with a simple thank you to someone who had not been kind.
teachings.quote: Since we have stayed in his house, don’t we have to thank him?
teachings.ch: Ch. 3, "Put My Mind at Peace", pp. 37-38
teachings.take: Send a short thank-you message today to someone you would not normally thank.
reflects: Who has helped you, even reluctantly, that you have not thanked?
How do you usually respond to people who judge you unfairly?
Why do you think Swamishri insisted on meeting Jashbhai?
What might gratitude soften in a difficult relationship of yours?
When has a small courtesy changed how someone saw you?
What are three things you are grateful for today?
Is there someone you have written off too quickly?
How does it feel when someone thanks you unexpectedly?
What sometimes stops you from saying thank you?
Who could you thank after an interview or meeting this week?
teachings.reflect: Who has helped you, even reluctantly, that you have not thanked?

teachings.title: Please help me further
parts: When Yogiji Maharaj passed away in 1971, the sadhus closest to him were heartbroken. In the quiet days that followed in Gondal, Pramukh Swami Maharaj sat with a few of them on the cement seat around a tree. The talk was brief and hushed. Then, unexpectedly, he said that Yogiji Maharaj had given them all the responsibility of serving Satsang, the spiritual fellowship, and asked them to keep helping him as they always had.

He spoke to them as equals, calling them his godbrothers, fellow disciples of the same guru. The sadhus were taken aback. To them he was already their guru, and they told him so, asking him to care for them and forgive their weaknesses as Yogiji Maharaj had done. He made no claim to authority at all. He simply asked for help, and said they would have to work together.

Mahant Swami later admitted that when Yogiji Maharaj left, he felt everything was over. Yet before he knew it, he found himself deeply bound to Pramukh Swami Maharaj. Asking for help did not make the new leader smaller; it drew people closer. Beginning something new, whether a role or a search, is lighter when you let others carry some of it with you.
teachings.quote: We will all have to get together and work.
teachings.ch: Ch. 4, "Yogiji Maharaj Has Not Left Us", pp. 46-47
teachings.take: Ask one person for one specific piece of help with your job search this week.
reflects: What are you trying to carry alone at the moment?
Who could you ask for help, and with what exactly?
How do you feel about asking for help?
What do you notice about the way Swamishri asked?
When has someone asking for your help made you feel valued?
Who are the fellow travellers in your life right now?
What would working together look like for one of your goals?
How could you let someone share your search without feeling a burden?
When has a loss eventually led you somewhere good?
What message could you send today to ask for support?
teachings.reflect: What are you trying to carry alone at the moment?

teachings.title: The water did not reach them
parts: As a child in Chansad, Shantilal listened to the village priest describe the holy men of the Himalayas, and dreamed of living in Haridwar. Life took a different path, and he accepted it as God's wish. In 1987, aged 67, he finally walked the ghats (riverside steps) of Haridwar with a pilgrimage group of 450, feeling like that young aspirant again. He wanted every pilgrim to gain as much as possible.

Standing in the Ganga, he bathed Harikrishna Maharaj, the small murti (sacred image) of God he always carried, then scooped water in his hands and sprinkled it over the group, making sure no one was missed. Some sadhus had crossed to the far bank for a better view, and shouted that they had been left out. Chuckling, he bent low and flung water towards them with all his strength.

Of course the water never crossed the river, yet those sadhus almost danced with joy, because they had not been forgotten. Then he beckoned, about thirty swam over, and others jumped from a bridge while he laughed and patted each head that floated past. If you ever feel stuck on the far bank, remember that love crosses distances water cannot.
teachings.quote: The water did not of course reach them, but Swamishri’s love had.
teachings.take: If you feel left out today, send one message to someone who might feel the same.
reflects: Where in your life do you feel like you are on the far bank?
Who might be feeling left out that you could reach towards?
What childhood dream of yours turned out differently?
How does it feel to imagine being remembered across a distance?
What moment of simple joy with others do you treasure?
What does 'accepting it as God's wish' mean to you right now?
When have you felt someone's love even when they could not be there?
Who makes sure you are not missed out?
What would you like to do with the dreams still waiting?
How could you make someone feel remembered this week?
teachings.reflect: Where in your life do you feel like you are on the far bank?

teachings.title: You are tired, go to sleep
parts: In the summer of 1988, Pramukh Swami Maharaj was touring America. The days were long and packed with devotees, meetings and decisions. One night in Atlanta he drifted off to sleep while his attendant sadhu gently massaged his legs. The attendant, just as worn out, nodded off too, his head coming to rest on Swamishri's feet.

Later that night Swamishri turned over and saw what had happened. He did not wake the young sadhu sharply or call for anyone. He cupped the sadhu's head gently in his hands and lowered it onto the mattress. The movement woke him and he sat up in a fluster, but Swamishri only told him kindly that he was tired, and should go to sleep.

There is no reproach in those words, only permission. The sadhu had not failed at his seva (service); he was simply a person who needed rest, and in this story rest was exactly what his guru wanted for him. On nights when sleep will not come, or when you feel you have not done enough, imagine those hands and that voice.
teachings.quote: You’re tired. Go to sleep.
teachings.take: Tonight, choose a gentle bedtime and let yourself stop, without judging what you did or did not finish.
reflects: What would you do tonight if you gave yourself permission to rest?
Where do you feel you have to keep going even when tired?
Who tells you to rest, and do you listen?
How do you speak to yourself when you are exhausted?
What helps you wind down before sleep?
Can you picture Swamishri's hands and words as you lie down tonight?
What is one thing you could let go of today?
How might you show this gentleness to someone else?
What would a calm evening routine look like for you?
When did you last feel truly rested?
teachings.reflect: What would you do tonight if you gave yourself permission to rest?

teachings.title: When you feel like a burden
parts: Chaturbhuj Swami had served the mandir at Atladra faithfully for over forty years, so careful that he could not bear to see a single penny wasted. In old age his kidneys failed and he needed regular dialysis in hospital. No longer able to serve as before, he felt useless to the Sanstha (the organisation). He told Pramukh Swami Maharaj that he was only a burden, and asked for the treatment to stop.

Swamishri was deeply moved. He answered quietly that the dialysis must continue, and that if need be he would visit two more villages. He meant he would add to his own already exhausting travels to ask devotees for help with the costs. He told the doctors and sadhus to spare no effort in keeping the old sadhu comfortable and well, and the treatment went on.

Chaturbhuj Swami measured his worth by what he could still do. Swamishri measured it differently: the man before him was precious simply as he was, and worth any extra effort. If the thought 'I am a burden' ever visits you, notice that it is a thought, not the truth, and let someone who loves you answer it.
teachings.quote: Continue the dialysis. I will tour two more villages if need be.
teachings.take: If you feel like a burden today, tell someone you trust, and let them answer.
reflects: What do you believe gives a person worth?
Who in your life would go the extra mile for you?
When have you measured yourself only by what you can do?
How do you treat others who are unwell or unable to work?
Could you offer yourself that same kindness?
Who could you tell honestly if you ever felt like a burden?
What would someone who loves you say to that thought?
How does it feel to receive care without earning it?
Which part of this story stays with you?
What is one way you are valued that has nothing to do with being productive?
teachings.reflect: What do you believe gives a person worth?

teachings.title: No notes of failings
parts: Pramukh Swami Maharaj could be firm with his sadhus when they drifted from their ideals. Yet the book is clear that, whatever their lapses, he was always ready to forgive and forget. Explaining a passage of the Vachanamrut (the recorded teachings of Bhagwan Swaminarayan) in Mumbai, he assured his listeners that God and his Sadhu keep no record of a person's failings; if they did, nobody would ever be liberated.

A sadhu in Bochasan once asked him a searching question. Swamishri gave them such lofty teachings, yet they could not live up to them; did he never feel frustrated? His answer was full of patience. A soul is only a soul, he said, and what matters is that it has turned towards God. Shriji Maharaj himself was compassionate, and one day that soul will become brahmarup, godly in nature.

He added that it is no small thing to have come into divine company at all. This is not a teaching that excuses carelessness, but it lifts a heavy weight. You are not being watched for mistakes. You are being walked with, slowly and patiently, towards the good, by someone who has already decided to keep no notes.
teachings.quote: God and his Sadhu keep no notes of a person’s failings.
teachings.take: When you replay a mistake today, say quietly 'no notes are being kept', and take one kind step.
reflects: Which of your own mistakes do you keep notes on?
How does it feel to hear that God keeps no such record?
What would change if you believed you were being walked with, not watched?
When have you forgiven someone without keeping score?
Which ideal do you find hard to live up to right now?
How could you be as patient with yourself as Swamishri was with the sadhus?
What small sign shows you have turned towards God?
Who in your life does not hold your past against you?
What would you like to put down today?
How would you speak to a friend who felt they kept falling short?
teachings.reflect: Which of your own mistakes do you keep notes on?

teachings.title: The worry that was not needed
parts: In 1966 Yogiji Maharaj was due to travel from Limdi to Rajkot. Pramukh Swami Maharaj sent the attendant sadhus ahead early to prepare lunch, and told them to go straight there. On the way they could not resist a quick detour for darshan (a sacred viewing of the murtis) at the historic mandir in Muli, built by Bhagwan Swaminarayan. They reckoned they could make up the time.

Then everything went wrong. Their roof rack caught on a low railway bridge and was ripped off, scattering pots and ladles across the road. A few kilometres later their tired old car broke down, and they had to be towed by another. They reached Rajkot hours late, and worry gnawed at them. Yogiji Maharaj would be waiting, and what would Pramukh Swami say?

They walked in to find Yogiji Maharaj calmly eating while Pramukh Swami sat beside him, lovingly serving. Seeing the attendants had not arrived, he had quietly cooked the whole meal himself. Yogiji Maharaj glowed with pleasure. The scene they had dreaded on the road was simply not there. So often the disaster we rehearse on the way is not what we find.
teachings.quote: Worry gnawed at them. What would Pramukh Swami say?
teachings.take: When you catch yourself rehearsing a disaster, name one other way the scene might turn out.
reflects: What are you worrying about in advance at the moment?
When has something you dreaded turned out fine?
How do you react when plans go wrong one after another?
What would you have felt in the car on the way to Rajkot?
Who quietly covers for you when things go wrong?
How could you do the same for someone else?
What helps your mind come back to the present when it races ahead?
What worry could you write down and set aside tonight?
How do you imagine Pramukh Swami greeted the late attendants?
What small mistake could you forgive yourself for today?
teachings.reflect: What are you worrying about in advance at the moment?

teachings.title: Do your utmost, leave the rest
parts: Yogiji Maharaj often spoke of Satsang spreading across the world, which to many devotees sounded like a dream. Pramukh Swami Maharaj took every word seriously and patiently built weekly assemblies abroad, some starting with only a handful of people. The effort was enormous. The book explains how he carried it: he saw himself as a servant and an instrument in God's hands. His part was to try; the results he left to God and guru.

On his first tour abroad as guru in 1974, he worked tirelessly, spending hours consoling families newly arrived in Britain from Uganda, settling disputes large and small, and speaking twice a day. When it ended there was still much to be done, and he knew he would need to return. Yet he felt no unease about leaving. He had given everything he could, and trusted Maharaj with what remained.

This is a freeing way to work, especially during a job search. You cannot control who replies, who is shortlisted, or when. You can control whether you tried honestly today. Do that part as fully as you can, then open your hands and let God hold the outcome, the way Swamishri did at the end of every tour.
teachings.quote: He had done his utmost, Maharaj would look after the rest.
teachings.take: At the end of today, name one thing you did your best at, then hand the rest to Maharaj.
reflects: Which outcomes are you trying to control at the moment?
What is fully in your hands today?
How does it feel to think of yourself as an instrument rather than the one in charge?
When have you done your best and still had to wait?
What would 'leaving the rest to Maharaj' look like in practice?
How do you usually feel after sending an application?
What helps you let go at the end of the day?
Who in your life models calm effort?
What is one honest effort you can make before bedtime?
How might your days feel if results were not your burden?
teachings.reflect: Which outcomes are you trying to control at the moment?

teachings.title: You carry your shoes, I'll carry mine
parts: In 1972 a pilgrimage train carried Pramukh Swami Maharaj, sadhus and devotees to Ayodhya. From there they set off by bus for Chhapaiya, the village where Bhagwan Swaminarayan was born. On the way, a broken bridge over a canal stopped them completely, and nobody knew what to do. Then a small, weary coal train came chugging towards Chhapaiya, and a few sadhus waved their shoulder cloths until the driver stopped.

Swamishri called for everyone to get on, and the whole group ran for it. He hitched his dhoti above his knees, grabbed his mojdi (sandals) in one hand and ran with them. When a sadhu offered to carry his sandals, a puffing Swamishri told him to carry his own and just keep running. Later the devotees felt bad they had not given him better transport, but he did not mind; his joy lay in reaching Chhapaiya for darshan.

On another trip in the monsoon, his tractor sank in the mud; a second and a third tractor sank too, before a fourth finally pulled it free, while he stood calmly and patiently to one side. Plans collapse and bridges break. His response was never panic, only good humour and the next practical step.
teachings.quote: You carry your shoes and I’ll carry mine… Just run!
teachings.take: When a plan falls through today, look for the next small train, and laugh a little as you run.
reflects: What plan of yours fell through recently?
How do you usually react when things break down?
What made Swamishri's response so light?
When has a detour turned into a good memory?
Who helps you laugh when things go wrong?
What is the 'next small train' in your situation?
How could you carry your own load without feeling alone?
What does calm patience look like for you on a stressful day?
What part of this story made you smile?
How might you tell today's setback as a funny story one day?
teachings.reflect: What plan of yours fell through recently?

teachings.title: Bored of what?
parts: Pramukh Swami Maharaj's days were crowded with letters, meetings, home visits and assemblies, often running late into the night. In 1994, at a youth camp in Atlanta, a young man asked him a very honest question: didn't he ever get bored with all this work? It is a question many of us quietly ask about our own routines, especially when days feel repetitive and purpose feels far away.

Swamishri answered at once, asking what there was to be bored of: this was why he had come. He explained that when we do something only because our own mind wants it, boredom follows. But when we act because the Satpurush (the God-realised guru) has asked, and we sincerely wish to please God, boredom never arrives. The meaning behind the work changes how the work feels.

During the long drought of 1987 and 1988, a seventy-year-old farmer, Megha Bapa, served twelve hours a day at one of the Sanstha's cattle camps. Asked if he ever grew tired or bored, his eyes filled: if Swami never tired of his huge work, why should he tire of his small one? Ordinary tasks, offered to God, can carry that same light.
teachings.quote: If we sincerely desire to please God and his Sadhu then boredom never comes.
teachings.ch: Ch. 7, "Neither Night, Nor Day", p. 99; Ch. 15, "A Friend in Need", p. 294
teachings.take: Before a dull task today, quietly offer it to Maharaj and notice if it feels different.
reflects: Which part of your day feels most repetitive?
What would change if you offered that task to God?
When have you done something dull that still felt meaningful?
What purpose would you like your days to serve?
How do you usually respond to boredom?
Whose example, like Megha Bapa's, inspires you?
What small task could you do today purely as seva?
How is job searching different when you see it as part of a bigger purpose?
What gives your day a sense of 'this is why I am here'?
How can you tell the difference between boredom and tiredness in yourself?
teachings.reflect: Which part of your day feels most repetitive?

teachings.title: Held since your forefathers
parts: In Nairobi in 1994, a devotee named Prakashbhai came to see Pramukh Swami Maharaj after breakfast. He was hoping for a photograph of Swamishri holding his hand, and asked him playfully to hold on. Swamishri replied, with a gentle smile, that they had been holding on since the days of his forefathers.

Then, to Prakashbhai's amazement, he recited the family line from memory: Prakash, son of Navnitbhai, son of Purushottambhai, son of Prahaladbhai, then Himmatsinh, then Haribhai, whose name appears in the Bhaktachintamani, an early account of Bhagwan Swaminarayan's life. He had held that family's hand ever since. The connection had not begun with the photograph; it reached back through generations.

In the same chapter, walking round a shrine in Sarangpur, he spotted an ordinary villager and called him by name: Vitthal, a potter who had briefly served there forty years before. You may feel you have only just reached out, or that your grip is weak. But you were being held long before you asked, and you are known by name.
teachings.quote: We’ve held on since the time of your forefathers,
teachings.take: When you feel unsteady today, open your palm for a moment and remember: your hand is already held.
reflects: Where do you feel your grip is weak at the moment?
How does it feel to know you were held before you asked?
Who in your family first brought you into Satsang?
What does it mean to you to be known by name?
When have you felt remembered by someone unexpectedly?
How could you hold someone else's hand this week?
What family blessings are you grateful for?
What would you say to Swamishri if you were holding his hand now?
How could this image help on an anxious day?
Who might need to hear that they are not forgotten?
teachings.reflect: Where do you feel your grip is weak at the moment?

teachings.title: It is me, Pramukh Swami
parts: In the assembly hall at Bochasan, devotees were waiting near the staircase. When Pramukh Swami Maharaj came down, everyone surged forward to surround him. He moved slowly through the crowd, patting bowed heads and smiling at faces he recognised. Only one man stayed seated: Manibhai, who was blind. He could hear the excitement, but could not get up and find his way without help, so he waited patiently where he was.

Through the crowd, Swamishri saw him and made his way across. He placed his hand lightly on Manibhai's head. Manibhai tilted his head back and asked who it was. Swamishri told him simply that it was Pramukh Swami. Manibhai could only gasp his name and say nothing more. There was no need to say anything. He had been seen, and remembered.

There are days when you cannot push forward with everyone else, when all you can do is sit where you are and wait. This story says that is enough. The one you are waiting for can see you, and will come across the room to you. You do not have to be first in the crowd to be reached.
teachings.quote: He had not been forgotten.
teachings.take: If you cannot do much today, simply sit quietly for two minutes and let yourself be found.
reflects: When have you felt unable to keep up with everyone else?
What does it feel like to picture Swamishri crossing the room to you?
Who in your life notices when you are left behind?
How could you notice someone who cannot push forward?
What does 'waiting patiently' look like for you on a heavy day?
When have you felt seen without having to ask?
What would you want to say if you were Manibhai?
How can you be gentle with yourself on days you can only sit still?
Who could you reach out to who might feel forgotten?
What small comfort can you allow yourself today?
teachings.reflect: When have you felt unable to keep up with everyone else?

teachings.title: The poor man's whole offering
parts: When devotees were pledging donations for a new mandir, Pramukh Swami Maharaj met them one by one. He asked about each person's income and responsibilities, such as loans, medical bills or a daughter's wedding, and together they settled on a sensible figure. A very poor devotee stood in the line, brimming with enthusiasm, and began to promise a large sum.

Swamishri gently asked about his situation and saw that he could not possibly manage it. He suggested a small offering, and that the rest be used to provide for his family and educate his children. The man insisted he would beg in the streets if he had to. Moved and pleased, Swamishri patted him; the devotion was already accepted. Talking quietly, he persuaded him to lower the amount a great deal, without hurting his feelings.

The book recalls how delighted Bhagwan Swaminarayan was when the aged, poor Dubli Bhatt offered just 13 paise for the Gadhada mandir. Maharaj explained that others had given large sums but still had plenty left, while Dubli Bhatt had given everything he had. God treasures the heart behind a gift, not its size. Your small offering of time, effort or love counts in full.
teachings.quote: His all! You have offered considerable sums, but still have other possessions.
teachings.take: Offer one small thing today, a prayer, a phone call or ten minutes of help, with your whole heart.
reflects: What do you feel you have to offer right now?
When have you felt your contribution was too small to matter?
How does Dubli Bhatt's story change that feeling?
What small offering could you make with your whole heart today?
Why do you think Swamishri cared about the man's family as well as his devotion?
Where could you give time or attention rather than money?
Who has given you something small that meant a great deal?
How can you honour the effort behind other people's gifts?
What does sincerity look like in your daily puja?
How might you value your own efforts more generously?
teachings.reflect: What do you feel you have to offer right now?

teachings.title: Thirty minutes of anger, then dinner
parts: In July 1985, twenty thousand people gathered in a London football stadium to honour Pramukh Swami Maharaj. Uncomfortable with the fuss, he spent his speech giving all credit to Bhagwan Swaminarayan and his gurus. That same night, at the house where he was staying, a middle-aged man asked to see him privately. Once inside, the man began shouting, worked himself into a fury, and poured out abuse and threats.

An attendant sadhu tried to have him removed. Swamishri stopped him, and quietly bore it all for a full thirty minutes, offering no argument and no defence. When the man finally left, spent and exhausted, Swamishri asked a sadhu to make sure he was given a meal before he went. Then he calmly picked up his pen and went back to answering letters.

The Bhagavad Gita describes a sthitapragna, someone who stays steady through both praise and insult. Within a few hours Swamishri received both, and neither shook him. Staying calm with an angry person is not weakness. Caring for someone even as they lash out is a strength most of us can only grow towards, one small moment at a time.
teachings.quote: Serve this man dinner, make sure he doesn’t leave hungry.
teachings.take: If someone speaks sharply to you today, take one slow breath before you reply.
reflects: How do you usually react when someone is angry with you?
What helps you stay steady when you feel attacked?
When have you been both praised and criticised in a short space of time?
What do you think the angry man felt when he left?
How could you respond more calmly in a family argument?
What does 'steady in praise and insult' mean to you?
Who in your life shows this kind of calm?
What is one breathing habit that settles you?
How can you be kind to yourself after a hurtful conversation?
What small step towards calm could you practise this week?
teachings.reflect: How do you usually react when someone is angry with you?

teachings.title: The ease of saying sorry
parts: After a large pilgrimage to the Himalayas, Pramukh Swami Maharaj received an angry letter from a man in London. His family had travelled on the same dates and struggled to find rooms. He accused Swamishri of being selfish and said the group had spoilt their holiday. In fact the trip had been carefully planned months ahead, and the clash was pure coincidence. Swamishri was in no way to blame.

Still, he wrote back with an apology. He said he was sorry for any inconvenience, that causing them distress had never been the intention, and that had the family told them at the time, rooms would gladly have been arranged. He did not defend himself or explain the planning. His apology was not an admission of guilt; it was a way of caring about how they felt.

Another time in New York, a seven-year-old named Yogi was speaking to him when Swamishri turned aside to talk with a sadhu. Yogi sat down, upset that nobody was listening. Swamishri apologised at once, admitted he had made a mistake, and asked the boy to stand and begin again. Whether at fault or not, a sincere sorry costs little and mends much.
teachings.quote: It was not our intention to cause you distress.
teachings.take: If someone is upset today, try 'I'm sorry that was hard for you' before explaining anything.
reflects: Is there an apology you have been putting off?
How do you feel when someone apologises to you simply and warmly?
What is the difference between saying sorry and blaming yourself?
Why do you think Swamishri did not explain the careful planning?
How did young Yogi probably feel when Swamishri said sorry?
When have you felt unheard, like Yogi?
How could you listen more fully to someone this week?
What makes an apology sincere to you?
Who could you ask to 'begin again' in a conversation?
How can you apologise without piling guilt on yourself?
teachings.reflect: Is there an apology you have been putting off?

teachings.title: You know, and I do not
parts: In Gondal, Pramukh Swami Maharaj was describing Satsang as joining one's hands humbly before the guru and following his guidance. Krishna Pandya, an old devotee who often joked with him, called out that he could manage the humble part. Swamishri teased back that the second part was harder: when the guru asks something, the mind gets upset. Except that he meant the English word 'upset', and it came out as 'except'.

As he tried again, a little boy piped up with the right word. Swamishri turned to the assembly, delighted, and praised the boy for speaking correctly. Then he told the child, with a smile, that the boy knew and he did not, because he had not studied as far. He was pleased the boy knew English, and not the least bit bothered at being corrected in front of everyone.

Being corrected can feel exposing, especially when you are already anxious about how you come across. Here a guru revered around the world was corrected by a small child in public, and his response was warmth and praise. Mistakes in front of others do not have to be humiliating. They can be a chance to lift someone else up.
teachings.quote: You know whilst I do not know.
teachings.take: When someone corrects you today, try saying 'Thank you, you're right' and notice how it feels.
reflects: How do you usually feel when someone corrects you?
What stood out to you about Swamishri's response?
When have you been embarrassed by a small mistake in public?
How could you turn a correction into a moment of warmth?
Who could you praise for knowing something you do not?
What would it feel like to say 'you know, and I do not'?
How does humour help when you make a mistake?
What are you still learning that you could admit openly?
How might this attitude help in a job interview?
Who taught you something recently, and have you thanked them?
teachings.reflect: How do you usually feel when someone corrects you?

teachings.title: No need to rush around
parts: In Hong Kong, Pramukh Swami Maharaj watched his attendant scurrying from room to room in a devotee's house, hunting for a cushion so that Swamishri would have a proper seat for lunch. Eventually he found one and invited him to sit. Afterwards Swamishri gently told him not to worry next time. There was no need to send others rushing about just for a seat; he would happily sit on the floor, as he had all his life.

In 1971 a devotee in Mumbai, Kishorbhai Dave, invited Swamishri to bless his new flat before the family moved in. Swamishri arrived on time, but they were not ready. The mattresses were down, the sheets were not. Kishorbhai ran about trying to do everything at once. Without a word, Swamishri began laying the sheets on the mattresses himself, leaving Kishorbhai embarrassed and deeply touched.

Anxiety often tells us that everything must be perfect before we are acceptable. These stories say otherwise. The people we most want to please are often not asking for perfection at all. When things are unfinished or you feel behind, it may be enough to slow down, breathe, and let someone help you lay the sheets.
teachings.quote: There’s no need to rush others around just for a seat.
teachings.take: Leave one thing slightly imperfect today on purpose, and notice that all is still well.
reflects: Where do you feel everything must be perfect before others see it?
How do you feel when you are caught unprepared?
What do you think Kishorbhai felt when Swamishri laid the sheets?
Who in your life is happy to help rather than judge?
What could you let be 'good enough' this week?
How does rushing affect your mood?
What would slowing down look like in your morning?
When have you been relieved that someone did not mind a mess?
How can you put a flustered person at ease?
What would you like to tell yourself when you feel behind?
teachings.reflect: Where do you feel everything must be perfect before others see it?

teachings.title: Not my burden but God's
parts: In London in 1994, a teenager asked Pramukh Swami Maharaj how he stayed so fresh amid so much activity. His answer was unusually personal. Whatever he did, he said, he did because he had been asked to by his gurus. The responsibilities belonged to God, not to him. And while he served, he kept remembering the murti (sacred form) of Maharaj and Swami.

In Houston, a devotee asked how he remained free of ego when sadhus praised him in assemblies. He replied that whatever happens is due to God's grace, and ego only creeps in when we feel that we are doing it all. When asked how often that awareness of God's grace came to him, he answered humbly that it never left him.

This can be a real relief for an anxious mind. We are asked to do our part sincerely, but we are not asked to carry the whole world on our shoulders. When the weight of a task, a search or a decision feels crushing, you can quietly hand the load back to the one it truly belongs to, and simply do the next thing.
teachings.quote: The responsibilities are not my burden but God’s.
teachings.ch: Ch. 9, "Panch Vartman", p. 169; Ch. 10, "God First", p. 176
teachings.take: When a task feels heavy today, say 'This is Yours, Maharaj; I will do my part' and begin.
reflects: What responsibility feels heaviest to you right now?
How would it feel to hand that weight back to God?
What is 'your part' in that situation?
When do you notice the feeling 'I have to do it all'?
How might remembering Maharaj while you work change your mood?
When has something worked out that you could not have managed alone?
How could you remember God's grace during a busy day?
What would you stop worrying about if you trusted God as the doer?
How does this teaching sit with your own sense of effort?
What is the next small thing you can do, and leave the rest?
teachings.reflect: What responsibility feels heaviest to you right now?

teachings.title: Remembering him all day
parts: A devotee in Bochasan once asked Pramukh Swami Maharaj an innocent question. All day long he patiently met people and listened to their troubles, so when did he find time for bhakti (devotion)? Swamishri laughed. He said he did bhakti without a break: every moment he thought of Maharaj and Swami, and alongside that he served people, because he had come to ease the distress of those who were unhappy.

The devotee had thought of devotion as something done at set times, such as arti, puja or turning the mala (rosary). He learned that the deepest devotion is an unbroken closeness to God that runs quietly beneath everything else. When someone else asked how he managed to remember Harikrishna Maharaj all day, Swamishri said it was because God takes such care of us; how could we not remember him?

That turns the usual pressure around. Remembering God is not another task to squeeze into a crowded day, but a natural response to being cared for. You can remember him while sending an application, helping at home or walking to the shops. A single thought of gratitude in the middle of an ordinary moment is already bhakti.
teachings.quote: He takes so much care of us, how can we not remember him?
teachings.take: Set a gentle reminder three times today to think: 'He takes care of me.'
reflects: When in your day do you feel closest to God?
What ordinary task could become a moment of remembrance?
How has God cared for you this week?
Do you think of bhakti as something only done at set times?
What helps you return your thoughts to Maharaj?
How might serving others be a form of devotion for you?
What would an unbroken sense of closeness feel like?
When do you most easily forget God, and why?
What small reminder could you place where you will see it?
How does it feel to think of remembrance as gratitude rather than duty?
teachings.reflect: When in your day do you feel closest to God?

teachings.title: Show it to Thakorji first
parts: In Kisumu, Kenya, Pramukh Swami Maharaj visited a doctor's surgery for a vaccination. The doctor handed him a pill to take beforehand. Swamishri immediately asked that it first be shown to Thakorji, meaning Harikrishna Maharaj, the murti of God he always kept close. The pill was held before the murti for a few moments, and then, quite naturally, he swallowed it.

The doctor knew that everything Swamishri ate was first offered to God, and had heard that even new shoes and glasses were shown to Thakorji. But medicine was new to him. After his cataract operations in Boston, Swamishri did the same with his new spectacles: he had them presented to Thakorji, then asked for the murti to be brought, so that his first sight through the new lenses was darshan of the Lord.

It is a lovely, simple practice. It does not replace doctors or treatment; Swamishri took his medicine and wore his glasses. It invites God into the ordinary business of looking after ourselves. Tablets, appointments and fresh starts can all be shown to Thakorji first, and received back as something blessed.
teachings.quote: Show it to Thakorji first,
teachings.take: Before taking your tablets today, hold them before Thakorji for a moment, then take them as usual.
reflects: What everyday things could you show to Thakorji first?
How might this practice change how an appointment feels?
What new start in your life would you like to offer to God?
How does it feel to think of treatment as something blessed?
What did you notice about how natural Swamishri was about this?
Which daily routine could include a moment of offering?
How do you feel about looking after yourself as a form of devotion?
What would you like your first 'darshan' of each day to be?
Who helps you take care of yourself, and how can you thank them?
What small ritual brings you calm?
teachings.reflect: What everyday things could you show to Thakorji first?

teachings.title: Darshan from a hospital bed
parts: In April 1986, surgeons in Mumbai removed a large growth from Pramukh Swami Maharaj's thigh; tests had already shown it was harmless. As he came round, still drowsy, someone slipped his glasses on and another held up what had been removed. Swamishri was not interested. His first question was where Maharaj was. When Harikrishna Maharaj was brought to him, he folded his hands in prayer.

The doctors and attendants urged him to rest and withdrew to a corner. He tried to sleep but could not. Instead, for about twenty minutes, they watched him fold his hands, speak softly, listen and smile. Days later the sadhus asked what he had been doing. He admitted he had been having darshan of the murtis in all their mandirs: Sarangpur, Gadhada, Gondal, Ahmedabad and more.

He could not travel, so he travelled inwardly. Worship held in the mind and heart like this is known as mansi puja. On days when you cannot get to the mandir, when you are tired, unwell or simply stuck at home, you can still close your eyes and visit each shrine you love, one by one, from wherever you are.
teachings.quote: I was doing darshan of the murtis in all our mandirs.
teachings.ch: Ch. 10, "God First", pp. 189-190; Ch. 16, "Spiritual Teachings Made Simple", pp. 306-307
teachings.take: Tonight, close your eyes and visit one mandir in your mind, murti by murti.
reflects: Which mandir would you most like to visit in your mind tonight?
How could mansi puja help on days you cannot go out?
What was Swamishri's first thought on waking, and what is yours?
How does it feel to know darshan is possible from anywhere?
Which murti do you picture most clearly?
When have you felt close to God while unwell or tired?
What would you say to Maharaj during your inward darshan?
How might this practice help you fall asleep?
Who could you share this practice with?
What does it mean to you that God can be visited in the heart?
teachings.reflect: Which mandir would you most like to visit in your mind tonight?

teachings.title: Then you do believe in God
parts: In Bochasan a father brought his teenage son to Pramukh Swami Maharaj with a complaint: the boy did not believe in God. The teenager had not wanted to come at all; his parents had almost dragged him from the house. He stood silently, bracing himself for a telling-off. Swamishri was not shocked in the slightest. Many people, after all, do not believe in God.
