Instead he asked a few simple questions. Did the boy live an ethical life? Yes. Did he do wrong? No. Any addictions, meat or alcohol? No. Then, Swamishri concluded warmly, he did believe in God. He added that just as we keep some rules out of respect for the law or community, we can live knowing God sees us, and that trusting God as the doer brings strength and courage.

The teenager bowed his head for a pat of blessing, feeling that here was someone who truly understood him. Faith is not always loud or certain. Sometimes it is already there, quietly, in how you try to live. If your faith feels thin on a heavy day, look at your choices; they may be believing more than you realise.
teachings.quote: Then you do believe in God!
teachings.take: List three good choices you made this week, and see them as quiet acts of faith.
reflects: When does your faith feel thin?
Which of your everyday choices show what you believe?
How do you think the teenager felt when he was not scolded?
Who in your life understands you without judging?
What gives you strength and courage when you feel unsure?
How could you respond kindly to someone who doubts?
What does 'God sees me' mean to you in a comforting way?
When have you acted from faith without calling it that?
How do you like to be spoken to when you are struggling?
What quiet sign of faith do you notice in yourself today?
teachings.reflect: When does your faith feel thin?

teachings.title: When faith and results do not match
parts: In Los Angeles a young man came to Pramukh Swami Maharaj feeling depressed and frustrated. He had been in Satsang for years and kept all the niyams (the disciplines of devotee life), yet had found no success in business or in jobs. He admitted he was beginning to lose faith in religion itself. Swamishri put down the letter he was writing and leaned forward in concern.

There was no need to lose faith, he said. Krishna himself was with the Pandava brothers, and still hardship came to them. Dada Khachar, one of Bhagwan Swaminarayan's dearest devotees, had a land dispute that only the king of Bhavnagar could settle. Each time he went, Maharaj blessed him, yet it was not resolved in Maharaj's lifetime. Through it all, Dada never lost his faith or his love.

Swamishri told the young man not to become sad, and not to lose hope, but to pray to God and try his best. Faith is not a contract promising quick results. It is a relationship that keeps you company while you keep trying. A long wait for a job, or for anything, does not mean you have been forgotten.
teachings.quote: don’t lose hope. Pray to God and try your best
teachings.take: Today, pray one honest line about your job search, then do one practical thing towards it.
reflects: Where do you feel your efforts are not being rewarded?
How has this affected your faith, honestly?
What does Dada Khachar's patience teach you?
How can faith keep you company rather than feel like a test?
What is one prayer you could say about your job search?
What is one practical step you could take alongside it?
Who could you talk to when you feel like giving up?
When has a long wait eventually led somewhere good?
How would you encourage a friend in the same position?
What small hope can you hold onto this week?
teachings.reflect: Where do you feel your efforts are not being rewarded?

teachings.title: Peace because you came
parts: After a misunderstanding, a young man felt so hurt that he stopped coming to Satsang altogether. He said he wanted nothing more to do with the mandir, the sadhus or the devotees, and that no one there deserved his respect. His father came to Pramukh Swami Maharaj close to tears. Swamishri did not criticise the son at all. Instead, he spoke warmly of him and praised him.

The father went home and repeated those kind words. They softened the young man, and the next day he came to see Swamishri and broke down crying in his lap. Stroking his head, Swamishri told him not to be so upset, because seeing him unhappy made Swamishri unhappy too. He asked him to try to let the incident go, reminded him that Satsang is family, and said to come straight to him if anything like this happened again.

Then he said something remarkable: he felt so much peace that day, simply because the young man had come. Ever since hearing about him, Swamishri had been anxious. When we pull away after being hurt, we can imagine no one notices. This story says the opposite. Someone is waiting, not to judge, but to welcome you home.
teachings.quote: I feel so much peace today because you came…
teachings.take: If you have drifted from someone or somewhere, send one small message today.
reflects: Is there a place or person you have drifted from after being hurt?
How do you think the young man felt when he heard Swamishri's kind words?
Who might be quietly waiting for you to come back?
What makes it hard to return after a misunderstanding?
How could you speak kindly of someone who has pulled away?
What does 'Satsang is family' mean to you?
When have you been welcomed back without being judged?
Who could you go to directly if you felt hurt again?
What would it feel like to know your presence brings someone peace?
What small step back towards connection could you take?
teachings.reflect: Is there a place or person you have drifted from after being hurt?

teachings.title: Once you start, strength follows
parts: At a student hostel in Vidyanagar, a young man named Sandeep told Pramukh Swami Maharaj that he hesitated to apply the tilak-chandlo, the sacred mark devotees put on the forehead during morning puja. Nobody was stopping him. He simply felt he ought to wait until he had improved himself and was living the disciplines properly. Only then would he feel worthy to wear it.

Swamishri turned this round. His life would become ordered, he said, when he started wearing the tilak-chandlo, and once he began he would find the inner strength to keep going. The practice was not a prize for being perfect; it was a tool for becoming steadier. Elsewhere he compared a new routine to a young ox learning to wear a yoke: awkward at first, then natural once its neck grows strong.

He applied the same image to daily puja, reading and visiting the mandir: hard for a newcomer, but after a while it all comes naturally and the mind grows stable. If you are waiting to feel ready before beginning a routine, you may wait a long time. Begin small today. The strength tends to arrive after the first step, not before.
teachings.quote: Once you start you will gain the mental strength to continue.
teachings.ch: Ch. 11, "With Satsangis", pp. 214-215; Ch. 16, "Spiritual Teachings Made Simple", pp. 304-305
teachings.take: Choose one part of your morning routine and do it today, even if you do not feel ready.
reflects: What are you waiting to feel ready for?
Which small habit would you like to start this week?
How does it feel to hear that strength comes after starting?
What routine once felt awkward but now feels natural?
What is the smallest possible version of your new habit?
How could daily puja help your mind feel steadier?
What would you say to a friend who felt unworthy to begin?
When during the day would a new habit fit most easily?
How can you be patient while a habit is still new?
Who could encourage you to keep going for the first few weeks?
teachings.reflect: What are you waiting to feel ready for?

teachings.title: Even if you do not write
parts: When a young engineer, Mitesh Patel, moved to America at his relatives' urging, Pramukh Swami Maharaj asked him to write every month. Then he added a promise: even if Mitesh did not write, Swamishri would still write to him. He kept that promise. For nearly three years he sent regular letters, some more than twenty pages long, full of guidance from the Vachanamrut and stories of great devotees.

One letter speaks straight to anyone far from home and struggling. The surroundings may be tempting, he wrote, so take care. If difficulties come, do not lose heart, but be mindful not to repeat the same mistake. Do not give in; be bold and speak words of courage. If one is steadfast, God will surely help. And he added that they had prayed for Mitesh from where they were.

When life is heavy, it is easy to stop writing: to stop praying, calling or showing up. This story says the connection does not depend on you holding up your end perfectly. Someone keeps writing anyway, and keeps praying for you from where they are. When you are ready, even a few words back are enough to pick up the thread.
teachings.quote: Even if you don’t write, I’ll still write to you.
teachings.take: Write a short prayer or note to Swamishri today, even just one line.
reflects: Where have you 'stopped writing' lately, in prayer or friendship?
How does it feel to know someone keeps writing anyway?
What would you write back today, in one line?
Who prays for you, even from far away?
What difficulty are you facing where you need courage?
How could you avoid repeating a mistake without punishing yourself?
What does being steadfast look like for you this week?
Who could you write to who might need encouragement?
When have you felt far from home, and what helped?
What words of courage could you say to yourself today?
teachings.reflect: Where have you 'stopped writing' lately, in prayer or friendship?

teachings.title: The bench that collapsed
parts: In Ukai, an engineer at the great dam invited Pramukh Swami Maharaj to stay at his home and gathered colleagues for a small evening assembly. Swamishri sat in the middle of a broad bench, with Dr Swami and Mahant Swami on either side. When another sadhu arrived a little late, Mahant Swami insisted he squeeze onto the bench as well, and everyone shuffled along to make room.

With that, the bench gave way. Swamishri and the two senior sadhus flipped over backwards, heads down and feet in the air. The horrified engineers rushed to help him up, and found him laughing uncontrollably. The serious business of satsang had been in full flow, and then, whoosh, a backward somersault. His sense of humour saved the day.

Nearly twenty years later, at a convention outside Mumbai, a sadhu retold the story on stage. Swamishri, busy writing letters, burst out laughing, leaned back and raised his arms and legs to show everyone exactly how he had fallen. Embarrassing moments can become the stories we laugh about most, if we let them.
teachings.quote: He was laughing uncontrollably! He found the whole accident hilarious.
teachings.take: Think of one embarrassing moment from your past and let yourself smile at it today.
reflects: What embarrassing moment still makes you cringe?
Could you imagine laughing about it one day, as Swamishri did?
How does humour change a difficult situation?
Who in your life helps you laugh at yourself kindly?
What did you enjoy most about this story?
How do you usually react when something goes comically wrong?
When did you last laugh until you could not stop?
How could you bring more lightness into a serious day?
What would change if you treated small accidents as funny rather than shameful?
Who could you share a funny memory with this week?
teachings.reflect: What embarrassing moment still makes you cringe?

teachings.title: Seventeen beginnings
parts: The youth assembly in Ahmedabad has an unusual record: it was launched seventeen times before it finally took root. Over several years, Yogiji Maharaj would appoint a committee, show them how to run the weekly gathering, encourage and bless the young people, and move on. Within a couple of weeks he would hear it had stopped. On his next visit he simply started again.

Sixteen times it fell apart, and the book says he watched it happen with great patience. By the mid-1980s, the Ahmedabad youth assembly had become one of the most active anywhere, with hundreds of young people filling the mandir hall. Pramukh Swami Maharaj carried on the same encouragement, and by the great festivals of 1981 and 1992, many thousands of young volunteers were serving.

A job search can feel like the Ahmedabad assembly: you start, it fizzles out, you start again. That does not mean you are failing. You may simply be on beginning number six, or eleven, or sixteen. Yogiji Maharaj's patience suggests that no fresh start is wasted. Each one is part of how something lasting is built.
teachings.quote: It had the distinction of being inaugurated seventeen times
teachings.take: If something has fizzled out, restart it today in the smallest possible way.
reflects: What have you started more than once?
How do you feel about restarting something that stopped?
What does Yogiji Maharaj's patience teach you?
Which beginning number do you think you are on in your job search?
What small restart could you make today?
Who encourages you when things fizzle out?
How could you be patient with a plan that keeps stalling?
What might be slowly taking root that you cannot see yet?
How would you encourage a friend on their tenth attempt?
What would it mean to see each fresh start as progress?
teachings.reflect: What have you started more than once?

teachings.title: Laughing all the way to Akshardham
parts: One evening in Mumbai, Pramukh Swami Maharaj took the small lift up to his fifth-floor room while the sadhus ran up the stairs. As the lift passed the third floor, they made loud chugging train noises and called out like station vendors. Upstairs they lined up as carriages, each holding the shoulder cloth of the one in front. Stepping out, Swamishri understood the game at once and became the engine.

He cheerfully appointed one sadhu to be the guard's van at the very back, and chugged off towards his room like a grandfather playing with his grandchildren. At his door he announced that the station had arrived and all carriages should separate. The sadhus were still giggling when he said, with a wave, that laughing and joking like this they would all surely reach Akshardham, the divine abode.

Another evening, a sadhu sat down right in his walking path to make him stop. Swamishri walked straight up to him, laughing, and leapfrogged clean over his head. He once said that once you have met God and his Sadhu, there is nothing left to do but laugh. Joy is not a distraction from spiritual life. It can be the very road.
teachings.quote: Happy and jesting in this way we’ll all surely get to Akshardham.
teachings.take: Find one small reason to laugh with someone today, and let it count as devotion.
reflects: When did you last play or be silly with people you love?
How does it feel to think of joy as part of spiritual life?
What part of this story made you smile most?
Who brings out the playful side of you?
How might laughter help on a heavy day?
What stops you from being light-hearted sometimes?
What simple game or joke could you share this week?
How could you make someone else laugh today?
What does it mean to you to be happy on the way to Akshardham?
When have you felt closest to others through laughter?
teachings.reflect: When did you last play or be silly with people you love?

teachings.title: Your genuine feelings are enough
parts: In 1991 a large Cultural Festival of India was held in Edison, New Jersey. Crowds of visitors parked in the surrounding streets, and some local residents grew angry, organised opposition and even printed their protest in a local newspaper. After the festival, a neighbour named Jim came to see Pramukh Swami Maharaj on behalf of the neighbourhood.

He apologised sincerely. They had come to love the festival and realised they had been wrong to cause such an uproar. They had even sent an official apology to the newspaper, he said, but it had not been printed, and he was truly sorry. Swamishri listened calmly and told him it did not matter whether the paper printed it or not. His sincere feelings were enough. God would be pleased, and Jim would find peace.

Swamishri did not ask for a public correction, or make Jim prove his regret. He received the apology as it was offered and let it be complete. When someone says sorry to you, you can do the same. And when you apologise and the world does not notice, remember that a sincere heart has already been seen.
teachings.quote: Your genuine feelings are enough for us.
teachings.take: If an apology is waiting to be accepted, receive it fully today, without needing more.
reflects: Is there an apology you have not fully accepted?
How do you feel when your sorry goes unnoticed?
What does it mean to let an apology be complete?
Why do you think Swamishri did not need a public correction?
When have you changed your mind about someone you once opposed?
How could you make it easier for others to apologise to you?
What would peace look like in a relationship that has been strained?
How can you trust that sincere feelings are seen by God?
What grudge could you gently set down this week?
How would you like to be treated when you admit you were wrong?
teachings.reflect: Is there an apology you have not fully accepted?

teachings.title: When a door closes
parts: The London Satsang community bought good land in Harrow to build a traditional mandir. After years of effort with the local authorities, permission was finally refused. Devotees were crushed, and for many the setback felt unbearable. The book notes that the person with most to lose was Pramukh Swami Maharaj himself. Yet when the news reached him by telephone, he stayed calm and composed.

To stop the devotees sinking into dejection, he immediately wrote them a nine-page letter. This had been the way since Maharaj's time, he explained: whatever God does is for our good. He described such moments as a test of faith and understanding, through which Maharaj makes us spiritually strong. Everything would turn out for the best, he assured them, so they must not lose heart.

Those words may have been hard to accept at the time. But in August 1995, a beautiful traditional stone mandir opened in Neasden, London. A no in one place became a far greater yes in another. When an application is rejected or a plan falls through, it is not the end of the story; it may simply be a turn in the road.
teachings.quote: Whatever he does will turn out for the best… Therefore don’t lose heart.
teachings.take: After any rejection this week, write 'This is not the end of the story', and rest.
reflects: What recent 'no' is still weighing on you?
How did you feel reading that Harrow became Neasden?
When has a closed door led you somewhere better?
What helps you stay calm when news is disappointing?
How could you encourage someone else after a rejection?
What does 'everything will turn out for the best' mean to you today?
Who writes you words of hope when you need them?
How can you care for yourself on the day a rejection arrives?
What might be growing that you cannot see yet?
What would you like to tell yourself about the next door?
teachings.reflect: What recent 'no' is still weighing on you?

teachings.title: Bring your certificates tomorrow
parts: While recovering from surgery at a devotee's home in Mumbai, Pramukh Swami Maharaj met a young labourer from Uttar Pradesh who had just delivered a basket of mangoes. Swamishri asked his name and what he did for a living. He carried baskets for a fruit merchant, he said, earning ten rupees a basket and rarely more than two deliveries a day. His clothes were worn and his parents were poor.

Swamishri asked whether he had studied. The young man said he had a qualification in homeopathic medicine, and had saved a little here and there to pay for the degree. But he had no money to open a dispensary, and after six months in the city he felt there was no one as unhappy as him. Tears welled in his eyes as he spoke.

Swamishri at once asked a sadhu to have devotee doctors find him work dispensing medicine, and told the young man to come back the next evening with his certificates. That same evening he personally asked the doctors to help. Being qualified but stuck is a painful place to be. One conversation, and one person willing to ask on your behalf, can change the direction of a search.
teachings.quote: Come here tomorrow evening with your certificates.
teachings.take: Get your certificates and CV ready today, as if someone has asked to see them tomorrow.
reflects: How do you feel about your own qualifications right now?
When have you felt stuck despite doing everything right?
Who could you tell honestly about your job search?
Who might be willing to ask on your behalf?
What would you want someone to notice about you?
How did Swamishri's questions help the young man open up?
What practical step could you take with your CV this week?
How might you help someone else who feels stuck?
What does it feel like to imagine being asked to bring your certificates?
What small hope can you carry into tomorrow?
teachings.reflect: How do you feel about your own qualifications right now?

teachings.title: Sit in the bhajan
parts: In the village of Sankari, Pramukh Swami Maharaj noticed several poor ploughmen sitting on a garden wall, chatting and smoking. Instead of passing by, he stopped to talk with them. He invited them to come to the mandir every day for darshan. The mandir was not only for the wealthier landowning families, he told them, but for them too, and he would be disappointed if others benefited while they did not.

He asked nothing of them but a few moments. If they sat for a little while in the mandir and joined the bhajan (devotional singing), he said, their weariness would lift. He was not asking for their money. In his eyes, simply coming to the mandir and joining their hands in prayer was worth as much as a gift of lakhs of rupees.

When you feel you have little to offer, or wonder whether you really belong, remember this invitation. The mandir is yours too. You do not need to arrive with anything but yourself. A few minutes of sitting, singing or listening can rest a weary heart, and your folded hands are treasured.
teachings.quote: sit in the bhajan and your weariness will go.
teachings.take: Put on one bhajan today and simply sit with it, hands folded, for its full length.
reflects: Do you ever feel you do not quite belong at the mandir?
How does it feel to hear 'the mandir is yours too'?
Which bhajan rests your heart most?
When did you last simply sit and listen, without doing anything else?
What weariness would you like to lay down today?
How could a few minutes in the mandir fit into your week?
What does it mean that folded hands are treasured?
Who could you invite to sit in a bhajan with you?
How do you feel after singing or listening to kirtan?
What would you like to offer, simply by being present?
teachings.reflect: Do you ever feel you do not quite belong at the mandir?

teachings.title: Giving back what you gave
parts: During the terrible drought of 1987 and 1988, the Sanstha opened camps to feed and shelter farmers' cattle. Four devotees from Sangavadar came to see Pramukh Swami Maharaj in Gondal. Things were miserable, they admitted, but they felt reluctant to send their bullocks to the camps. For years they had given their yearly offerings to the mandir. Now it felt wrong to be helped by it.

Swamishri asked them who had provided everything the mandir had. It was the devotees themselves, he said. They had sacrificed and given so much for Thakorji (God, as worshipped in the mandir). Now that they were in need, the mandir was helping them in turn. It was simply returning what they had given. There was no reason to hesitate, and he told them to send their bullocks to the camp at Bochasan.

Many of us find it far easier to give than to receive, especially when times are hard and we feel we ought to be coping alone. Accepting help is not a failure or a debt. Often it is the love you have given over the years, quietly finding its way back to you. Let it.
teachings.quote: We are giving you what you have given us!
teachings.take: Accept one offer of help this week without apologising for it.
reflects: Is it easier for you to give or to receive?
What help have you been reluctant to accept lately?
How have you given to others over the years?
What would it feel like to see help as love returning to you?
Who would be glad to support you if you let them?
What stops you from accepting help?
How do you feel when someone accepts your help gratefully?
What would you say to a friend who felt too proud to be helped?
How could you receive kindness this week without guilt?
What does 'Satsang is family' mean when you are the one in need?
teachings.reflect: Is it easier for you to give or to receive?

teachings.title: Sure of his teeth
parts: Each afternoon in Gondal, Pramukh Swami Maharaj would sit informally with the sadhus and share out prasad (blessed offerings). One day he gave half an orange to Ramji Bhagat, a young novice who was often gently teased. A sadhu joked that Ramji had teeth and could manage harder fruit. Swamishri, keeping a straight face, asked Ramji whether he really had teeth.

Ramji, who could never quite pronounce 'Swami', said he did. Could he see them? No. Then how did he know? Because he saw them in the mirror, Ramji insisted. Swamishri declared it must be a trick mirror; if he truly had teeth, he should be able to see them as plainly as his own palm! The whole room burst out laughing, Swamishri and Ramji loudest of all.

Ramji held his ground: his teeth could not be seen, but he definitely had them. Smiling broadly, Swamishri drew the lesson. We should be just as sure that we have found God's company. You may not always feel God near or see him plainly, but that does not make his presence any less real.
teachings.quote: We should have a likewise conviction of having attained the association of God.
teachings.take: When God feels far today, remind yourself: unseen does not mean absent.
reflects: When does God feel far away to you?
What makes you sure of something you cannot see?
How could Ramji's certainty help you on a doubtful day?
What signs of God's company have you noticed this week?
How does humour help you learn something deep?
What does 'unseen does not mean absent' mean to you?
Who in your life reminds you that God is near?
What part of this story made you laugh?
How could you hold on to faith when feelings are flat?
What would you like to feel sure of today?
teachings.reflect: When does God feel far away to you?

teachings.title: The note held high
parts: At a Rakshabandhan celebration, crowds pressed forward to have a rakhdi (sacred thread) tied by Pramukh Swami Maharaj. One young boy only wanted to touch him. Three times he rose on tiptoe, lost his balance and was swept aside by the jostling crowd. His hopes began to fade. Then he had an idea. He slipped away from the crush and scribbled a short note.

When the rush eased, he came back, stretched up on his toes and held the note high above his head with both hands. Swamishri noticed, bent down, took the note and blessed him, and the boy's joy knew no bounds. Back in his room, Swamishri read the scrap of paper and tucked it safely into his pagh (turban), keeping it for days.

Later he gently pointed out to a local sadhu that the high seating had kept him from the child. A lofty throne adds nothing to anyone's greatness, he said; far better to arrange things so that he and the children could meet freely. If you have tried and been pushed back, keep holding your note up. You will be seen.
teachings.quote: One’s greatness is in no way elevated by sitting on a high sinhasan.
teachings.take: Try once more today at something you gave up on, in a new way, like the boy's note.
reflects: Where have you tried and been pushed back?
What new way could you try to reach your goal?
How do you think the boy felt when Swamishri took his note?
What would you write on your note to Swamishri today?
When have you felt swept aside by a crowd, literally or not?
Who notices your efforts even when you feel small?
How could you make yourself more reachable to others?
What does it mean to you that Swamishri kept the note?
What hope are you still holding up?
How can you encourage someone who keeps getting pushed back?
teachings.reflect: Where have you tried and been pushed back?

teachings.title: No worry is too small
parts: Over the years, Pramukh Swami Maharaj read and answered hundreds of thousands of letters, around fifty a day, writing in the car, in waiting rooms and even between X-rays at the dentist. People wrote for inspiration, with questions or troubles, to unburden their hearts, or simply to say hello. He answered even the most trivial, and devotees treasured replies in his own handwriting as if he had visited their homes.

Some requests seem almost funny: blessings for a new well, advice on buying a scooter, what to do about a rickshaw that kept breaking down, or five anonymous postcards asking for hair to grow back. Others were weightier: how to stop noticing others' faults, how to keep faith at a difficult school. The book observes that what looks trivial to us may matter enormously to the person asking.

Swamishri understood this, and so he answered every one with patience. You never need to decide whether a worry is big enough for prayer, or for telling someone you trust. If it matters to you, it is worth bringing. Small worries, once spoken aloud, often lose some of their grip.
teachings.quote: Some write for inspiration; some write with questions, others with afflictions
teachings.take: Write down one small worry today and offer it to Maharaj, however minor it seems.
reflects: What small worry have you been keeping to yourself?
Do you ever feel your concerns are too minor to share?
Who listens to your small worries without judging?
What would you write in a short letter to Swamishri today?
How do you feel after you have told someone what is bothering you?
Which of the requests in this story made you smile?
How could you take someone else's small worry seriously this week?
What helps a worry lose its grip on you?
When is a good time each day to offer your worries in prayer?
What would it feel like to believe nothing you care about is too small for God?
teachings.reflect: What small worry have you been keeping to yourself?

teachings.title: He shook my hand
parts: After the 1991 festival in New Jersey, two teenagers who had served as exhibition guides went to meet Pramukh Swami Maharaj. Kalpesh wanted blessings for his further studies. His friend Mihir tagged along, nervous, because he had never met Swamishri privately before. When their turn came, Mihir went red in the face and ended up half bowing, half kneeling, unsure what to do.

Swamishri took his hand and shook it, asked him in English how he was, and then asked his name. Soon Mihir was introducing himself and felt completely at home. Outside on the lawn the two boys could not contain themselves; they leapt into the air, shouting that he had met them. Mihir could not get over it: Swamishri had shaken his hand and spoken to him in English.

At a youth camp in Ahmedabad, Swamishri listened just as warmly while a teenager named Mitul struggled bravely through a speech in Gujarati, almost willing him on. Nerves before a meeting or interview are normal. Kind people are rarely waiting for you to be polished. Many, like Swamishri, are quietly trying to help you feel at home.
teachings.quote: He met us, he met us!
teachings.take: Before your next call or interview, picture a warm handshake and a kind question.
reflects: What kinds of meetings make you most nervous?
How did Swamishri put Mihir at ease?
What would help you feel at home in an interview?
When has someone's kindness calmed your nerves?
How could you make a nervous person feel welcome this week?
What does 'being polished' mean to you, and does it matter as much as you think?
How do you usually introduce yourself when anxious?
What would you like an interviewer to know about you?
When have you struggled bravely through something, like Mitul?
What small joy could you celebrate afterwards, like the boys on the lawn?
teachings.reflect: What kinds of meetings make you most nervous?

teachings.title: Singing your way to stillness
parts: Kirtan bhakti is devotion through song. The book describes it simply: chanting God's holy names, and singing bhajans (devotional songs) about his divine actions, his virtues and his murti (sacred image), right down to his clothes and ornaments. It is one of the nine classical forms of bhakti, and it is open to everyone, whatever their voice sounds like and however much they know.

The book quotes the Shrimad Bhagvat, an ancient scripture, which says that in Kaliyug, our present age, the highest spiritual state can be reached through kirtan. That is a remarkable claim for something as ordinary as singing. It suggests God does not only meet us in silence, study and effort, but also in melody, in a tune hummed while getting ready for the day.

The book also explains why kirtan helps. Our senses and thoughts are easily pulled towards passing things. When we sing about God, they are gathered together and given somewhere good to rest. The result, it says, is peace, inner purity and tranquillity. A bhajan can be a gentle way of bringing a scattered mind back home.
teachings.quote: Kirtan bhakti results in peace, inner purity and tranquility.
teachings.ch: Ch. 5, "Swadharmanishtha: Bhakti I", Kirtan Bhakti, pp. 78-79
teachings.take: Put on one bhajan you love and sing along, even softly, before your day begins.
reflects: Which bhajan or kirtan do you find yourself humming most often?
When did singing last change how you felt inside?
Which part of Maharaj's life would you most like to sing about?
Do you prefer singing alone or with others? Why?
Which line of a kirtan has stayed with you for years?
How does your mind feel after five minutes of singing compared with before?
Is there a time of day when a bhajan would help you most?
Who taught you your first kirtan?
What stops you from singing more often, and could one small change help?
If you could only keep one bhajan, which would it be?
teachings.reflect: Which bhajan or kirtan do you find yourself humming most often?

teachings.title: The mantra that walks with you
parts: Among all the forms of kirtan, the simplest is the name itself. Bhagwan Swaminarayan gave his followers the Swaminarayan mahamantra, the great mantra of his own name. It needs no instrument, no book, no special place and no particular mood. It can be said aloud, whispered under your breath, or held silently in the mind while you do something else.

Gunatitanand Swami, the first guru in the succession after Bhagwan Swaminarayan, spoke about this mantra with great conviction. In the Swamini Vato, his recorded talks, he says there is no more powerful mantra today, that it loosens the pull of worldly desires, and that one should always chant it. In another talk he notes it can be chanted while moving around or walking.

This makes the mantra a companion rather than a task. It can travel with you to the shops, to an interview, or along a quiet evening walk. Each repetition is a small turning of attention towards God, woven into ordinary moments rather than set apart from them. Nothing about your day needs to stop for it.
teachings.quote: Today, there is no mantra more powerful than the Swaminarayan mantra.
teachings.ch: Ch. 5, "Swadharmanishtha: Bhakti I", Kirtan Bhakti, p. 79
teachings.take: On your next walk, silently repeat 'Swaminarayan' in time with your steps for one minute.
reflects: When do you most naturally remember to chant 'Swaminarayan'?
How does chanting feel different when walking rather than sitting still?
Is there a daily journey where the mantra could keep you company?
What does it mean to you that the mantra needs nothing but your attention?
Have you ever chanted the mantra in a worried moment? What happened?
Who in your family chants most often, and what have you noticed in them?
Would you rather chant aloud or silently? Why?
What is one ordinary task you could pair with the mantra this week?
How might it feel to think of the mantra as a companion rather than a duty?
What would you like the mantra to help you put down today?
teachings.reflect: When do you most naturally remember to chant 'Swaminarayan'?

teachings.title: Never tired of bhajans
parts: The Vachanamrut, the recorded discourses of Bhagwan Swaminarayan, contains a lovely personal admission. In Gadhada II 49 he says his mind never has enough of spiritual talks, devotional songs, conversations about God or meditation on him. However much there is, he wants more. Then he gently invites everyone listening to be the same.

It is striking that devotional songs sit on his list right beside discourse and meditation. Kirtan is not treated as a light extra or a warm-up before the serious part. It is one of the things God himself delights in, and the book presents it as one of the nine forms of bhakti with real spiritual value of its own.

The book carries this into seva, selfless service, too. Among its guidance on how to serve, it suggests remembering Maharaj and Swami and singing devotional songs while doing seva. Sweeping, setting out chairs or tidying a room can become a quiet form of worship when a bhajan runs alongside the work.
teachings.quote: My mind never becomes satiated with spiritual discourses, devotional songs
teachings.take: Next time you tidy or do a chore, hum a bhajan and let the work become seva.
reflects: What do you never tire of, and what does that say about what you love?
Which devotional song could you listen to again and again?
How does it feel to know Maharaj himself loved devotional songs?
Which everyday task could you pair with a bhajan?
Does singing make seva feel lighter for you? In what way?
When have you felt closest to God through music?
Is there a kirtan you would like to learn properly this month?
What might change if chores felt like offerings?
Who could you share a favourite bhajan with this week?
What does 'never satisfied' mean, in a good way, for you?
teachings.reflect: What do you never tire of, and what does that say about what you love?

teachings.title: Guarding a precious find
parts: Nishkulanand Swami was one of the paramhansas, the senior sadhus, of Bhagwan Swaminarayan, and a gifted poet. The book quotes his composition the Chosath Padi, a set of sixty-four verses. One line feels like a gentle hand on the shoulder: believe that you have received something exceptional, and do not let it slip out of your hands.

What is that exceptional thing? The book answers: the presence of Bhagwan Swaminarayan, the guidance of the Gunatit guru, and a path to God that it describes as rare even for the deities. The poet says to protect it day and night, whether sitting or sleeping, because something this valuable deserves care.

The book offers a simple picture. With only a few coins in your pocket, you might doze off on a train. With something truly valuable, you stay awake and keep a hand on it. Nishkulanand Swami's verse is less a warning than a reminder of worth: what you hold is precious, so hold it with love and attention.
teachings.quote: protect it day and night, while sitting and sleeping
teachings.take: Write down one thing about your satsang that feels precious, and keep it where you will see it.
reflects: What in your spiritual life feels most precious to you right now?
How do you usually look after the things you value?
What helps you remember your faith on busy or tired days?
Is there anything that quietly pulls you away from what you treasure?
Which kirtan line reminds you of how fortunate you are?
How might you 'keep a hand on' your faith during the week?
Who helps you protect what matters to you?
What is one small habit that guards your peace?
When did you last feel truly grateful for satsang?
If your faith were a jewel, where would you keep it?
teachings.reflect: What in your spiritual life feels most precious to you right now?

teachings.title: Now God comes looking
parts: For centuries, seekers in India went looking for God. The book describes people who endured great hardship, chanted God's name countless times and gave up comforts, all hoping to reach him. It recalls these long and difficult searches in order to set up a surprising and tender reversal that changes how the whole path looks.

In the Swamini Vato, Gunatitanand Swami says that in earlier times aspirants searched for God, but today God searches for the aspirants. The book explains that Bhagwan Swaminarayan came to earth out of compassion and remains present through the Gunatit guru, so the finding has already happened. God has found his devotees and drawn them close.

On days when you feel far away, lost or not good enough to reach God, this turns the picture around. You are not climbing an impossible mountain on your own. You are the one being sought. What remains is not to find him, but simply to recognise, a little more each day, that he is already near.
teachings.quote: today God searches for the spiritual aspirants
teachings.take: When you feel distant from God today, say quietly: 'He is looking for me too.'
reflects: When have you felt that God found you, rather than the other way round?
What does it feel like to imagine being sought instead of searching?
On a hard day, what makes God feel far away?
What might help you notice that he is already near?
Which person has been a sign of God reaching out to you?
When did satsang first feel personal to you?
What would you say to someone who felt too far away for God?
Is there something you have been trying too hard to earn?
Where in your day could you pause to recognise his closeness?
What small sign of care have you received recently?
teachings.reflect: When have you felt that God found you, rather than the other way round?

teachings.title: You are the one who watches
parts: Thoughts arrive whether we invite them or not. Some are kind and some are unsettling. The book explains that the mind has several aspects, one of which is the chitta, the part that dwells on thoughts and replays them. It is easy to believe that whatever passes through the chitta is simply who we are.

In Vachanamrut Gadhada II 6, Bhagwan Swaminarayan offers a different view. He teaches the realisation that I am distinct from the chitta: I am the atma, the soul, which observes it. Knowing this, he says, one should not become frustrated by the pure or impure thoughts that arise, but continue worshipping God and remain joyful.

This is a gentle and freeing idea. Thoughts can come and go like weather crossing the sky, while you are the one who watches. You do not have to win every argument with your mind or feel ashamed of what passes through it. You can notice a thought, let it pass, and turn back towards God.
teachings.quote: I am the atma, the observer of the chitta.
teachings.take: When an unsettling thought comes, silently call it 'just a thought', then gently carry on.
reflects: Which kinds of thoughts tend to visit you most often?
What changes when you picture a thought as passing weather?
How do you usually respond when an unwelcome thought arrives?
What would it feel like to watch a thought without arguing with it?
When have you felt calm even while your mind was busy?
What helps you turn back towards God after a difficult thought?
Which thought would you most like to hold more lightly?
How might you speak to yourself kindly after a restless moment?
What does 'I am the one who watches' mean to you?
What small practice could remind you of this during the day?
teachings.reflect: Which kinds of thoughts tend to visit you most often?

teachings.title: Nothing to worry about
parts: Many devoted people carry a quiet fear that their faults disqualify them. They notice their impatience, their low days or their unfinished habits and wonder whether God could really be pleased with someone so imperfect. The fear can become heavier than the faults themselves, and make prayer feel like standing in front of an examiner.

In Vachanamrut Gadhada II 13, Bhagwan Swaminarayan speaks directly to this fear. If a person has firm belief in God, he says, then even if a slight flaw remains, there is still nothing to worry about. The book places this among many teachings showing that faith in God is the foundation on which everything else rests.

This does not mean effort stops mattering. It means your standing before God is not measured by a spotless record. Faith is the ground you stand on, and imperfections are things you work on while standing there, held and unafraid. You can keep growing without being frightened of yourself. Slow progress is still progress.
teachings.quote: even if a slight flaw remains, there is still nothing to worry about
teachings.take: When you notice a flaw today, add the words: 'and God is still with me.'
reflects: Which of your imperfections do you worry about most?
How would you speak to a friend who worried in the same way?
What does it feel like to hear Maharaj say 'nothing to worry about'?
Where does your faith feel strongest right now?
How can you work on something without being harsh with yourself?
What would change if you believed your faults did not push God away?
Who in your life accepts you, flaws and all?
What is one small thing you are slowly growing in?
When have you felt loved despite a mistake?
What would you like to stop being frightened of in yourself?
teachings.reflect: Which of your imperfections do you worry about most?

teachings.title: A prayer for hard moments
parts: Sometimes we do not know what to say to God. The words will not come, or they come out tangled. The book shares two prayers from the Vachanamrut that Bhagwan Swaminarayan himself taught, ready-made words for the moments when our own run out. There is real comfort in knowing that the words we reach for were given to us by Maharaj himself, with our struggles already in mind.

In Gadhada I 48, he suggests praying to be protected from inner enemies such as anger, jealousy and egotism, and asking God to always grant us the company of his devotees. In Panchala 3, the prayer is tenderer still. It addresses God as one who intensely loves his devotees and as an ocean of mercy, then asks for protection, reminding us that we are distinct from the restless mind and senses.

What stands out is that Maharaj taught these prayers himself. He expected his devotees to struggle, and he wanted them to turn to him when they did. He said to pray like this daily, constantly. Asking for protection is not a sign of failure. It is exactly what he asked us to do.
teachings.quote: You intensely love your devotees! You are an ocean of mercy!
teachings.take: Tonight, say: 'O Maharaj, you are an ocean of mercy. Please protect me,' and rest there.
reflects: What words do you usually use when you pray?
How does it feel to call God 'an ocean of mercy'?
What would you most like protection from right now?
When have you felt a prayer answered, even quietly?
Whose company helps you feel closer to God?
Is it easier for you to pray in words or in silence?
How might a set prayer help on days when words will not come?
What does it mean to you that Maharaj expected his devotees to struggle?
What time of day would suit a short prayer for you?
If you wrote your own one-line prayer, what would it say?
teachings.reflect: What words do you usually use when you pray?

teachings.title: When prayer feels dry
parts: There are seasons when puja feels flat and meditation feels empty. You sit down to remember God and nothing seems to happen. No warmth, no stillness, just the same restless mind. It is easy to conclude that you are doing it wrong, or that God is not listening to someone like you.

Bhagwan Swaminarayan anticipated exactly this. The book summarises his guidance from the Vachanamrut: if, while meditating, a devotee cannot behold God's form within the heart even after a hundred years, he should still not lose courage or abandon the attempt, but keep trying. Elsewhere he says one should be ready to persevere patiently for a hundred years.

A hundred years is not meant as a burden. It is reassurance. Dry spells are expected. Feeling nothing is not the same as failing. The instruction is simply to keep coming back without losing heart, trusting that the returning itself matters to the one you are returning to. Coming back is enough.
teachings.quote: one should still not lose courage
teachings.take: If puja feels empty today, do it anyway for two minutes, and let that be enough.
reflects: When has your prayer or puja felt dry?
What usually helps you keep going when feelings are flat?
Does 'a hundred years' feel daunting or reassuring to you?
What is the smallest version of puja you could keep on hard days?
Who has shown you what steady faith looks like?
What would you say to a friend whose prayers felt empty?
Have you ever felt closeness return after a dry season?
What does 'not losing courage' look like for you this week?
Which part of your daily devotion do you most want to protect?
How can you be gentle with yourself when devotion feels distant?
teachings.reflect: When has your prayer or puja felt dry?

teachings.title: He asked to carry our pain
parts: The book returns again and again to one question: why did Bhagwan Swaminarayan come at all? He needed nothing from anyone. He was content and complete in himself. Yet he left home as a boy of eleven, travelled through forests and mountains, and then lived among people, all, the book says, for their sake.

One story captures this. In Vachanamrut Gadhada I 70 he asked for two boons. He asked that, instead of his devotees, he should suffer the pain of millions of scorpion stings. And he asked that, instead of them, he should be the one who had to survive by begging. He wanted their hardship to fall on him.

Other lines quoted in the book echo the same heart, including his words that to wish good for all is his natural tendency. On heavy days, it helps to remember that the God you pray to is not distant or indifferent. Out of love, he asked to take his devotees' suffering upon himself.
teachings.quote: To wish good for all is my natural tendency
teachings.ch: Ch. 1, "Swaminarayan Sadhana", pp. 3 and 7-8; Ch. 15, "Repaying Our Debt", p. 265
teachings.take: When something hurts today, remember that Maharaj once asked to bear his devotees' pain himself.
reflects: What does this story tell you about the God you pray to?
When have you felt cared for without having to ask?
Who in your life has tried to take on a burden for you?
How does it feel to know God wishes good for all?
What pain would you like to hand over to him today?
How might this story change the way you pray on hard days?
Which act of kindness towards you do you still remember?
In what small way could you lighten someone else's load this week?
What does 'he needed nothing, yet came for us' mean to you?
Where do you most need to feel held right now?
teachings.reflect: What does this story tell you about the God you pray to?

teachings.title: The one before the zeros
parts: Write a row of zeros on a page and it is worth nothing at all. Put a single 1 in front and suddenly every zero multiplies its value. Gunatitanand Swami used exactly this picture in the Swamini Vato, his recorded talks: God is the one, and sadhanas, our spiritual practices, are the zeros.

The book explains that practices such as study, pilgrimage, charity and discipline have real value, but only when they come after refuge in God and firm conviction in him. Without that 'one', they add up to nothing that truly frees the soul. With it in place, every effort counts and every zero adds to the total.

This is freeing. You do not have to measure your spiritual life by how many practices you pile up. Start with the one: your relationship with God. Then even small efforts, a single mala (round of prayer beads) or one line of the Vachanamrut, count for a great deal because of what stands in front of them.
teachings.quote: God is one and sadhanas are zeros.
teachings.take: Before any task today, pause to put the 'one' first: 'I do this for you, Maharaj.'
reflects: What is the 'one' at the front of your life right now?
Which of your efforts feel like zeros without God in front?
How does this picture change the way you see small practices?
What do you sometimes try to pile up in order to feel worthy?
Where do you feel God's presence most clearly?
What small effort could you offer to him today?
How would you explain the 'one and zeros' idea to a child?
When has faith made an ordinary action feel meaningful?
What helps you keep God first when life is busy?
What would it look like to measure your day by closeness, not quantity?
teachings.reflect: What is the 'one' at the front of your life right now?

teachings.title: It is only to mould me
parts: Near the end of the book, the author lists a handful of thoughts to hold daily so that spiritual practice stays steady through ups and downs. One of them is the thought that God is the all-doer. He suggests thinking that Bhagwan Swaminarayan and the guru are the doers of all, and that nothing happens without their wish, power and inspiration.

The thought continues: whenever, wherever and through whomever they act, it is solely for the happiness and wellbeing of me and others, and only to mould me. The book says that when this becomes firm, one stays stable and at peace through contradictory experiences, and even feelings of inferiority or superiority fall away.

For anyone in a season of waiting, of applications, silences and knock-backs, this is a gentle lens. It does not say you caused the setback or deserved it. It says the hand behind your life wishes you well, and that even what you did not choose can be shaping you towards something good.
teachings.quote: it is solely for the happiness and well-being of me and others
teachings.take: When something does not go your way today, whisper: 'This too is for my good.'
reflects: What setback are you finding hardest to accept right now?
How does it feel to believe God wishes you well within it?
When has something you did not choose ended up shaping you?
What would change if you stopped comparing yourself with others?
Where do you feel 'not enough' at the moment?
Who has God worked through to help you recently?
How might this thought change the way you read a rejection?
What do you hope God is moulding in you this year?
How do you tell the difference between accepting and giving up?
What is one thing you could hand over to him today?
teachings.reflect: What setback are you finding hardest to accept right now?

teachings.title: The single greatest endeavour
parts: Muktanand Swami, one of Bhagwan Swaminarayan's senior sadhus, once asked him a question that many seekers quietly carry. In Vachanamrut Gadhada I 33 he said: the shastras describe countless spiritual endeavours to please God, so which single one is so powerful that it earns as much of God's pleasure as all of them combined?

Maharaj's answer was simple. Accepting the firm refuge of God, he said, is the single greatest endeavour of all. The book notes that Muktanand Swami asked similar questions on other occasions, and the answers point the same way: bhakti joined with an understanding of God's greatness, and the company of a true Sant.

Refuge means taking shelter, the way someone steps in out of the rain. It is not a performance or an achievement. When the list of things you feel you should be doing grows long and heavy, this teaching puts one thing at the centre: turn to God and stay under his shelter. Everything else grows from there.
teachings.quote: Accepting the firm refuge of God is the single, greatest endeavour
teachings.take: When your to-do list feels heavy, say 'Maharaj, I take your refuge' before starting it.
reflects: What does 'taking refuge' mean to you in everyday life?
When do you most feel that you are sheltering in God?
What question would you have asked Maharaj if you had been there?
Which 'shoulds' in your spiritual life feel heaviest?
How might refuge feel different from effort?
Who first helped you learn to trust God?
What storms are you sheltering from at the moment?
How can you remind yourself of his shelter during a busy day?
What grows in you when you feel safe?
What is one simple way to renew your refuge each morning?
teachings.reflect: What does 'taking refuge' mean to you in everyday life?

teachings.title: Will this please Him?
parts: The book makes a striking point about this tradition. For a devotee, spiritual practice is not about finding God, because he has already been found. It is about earning his rajipo, meaning his pleasure or approval, and the rajipo of the guru. The whole of sadhana is reframed as a relationship rather than a search.

In Vachanamrut Gadhada II 28, Bhagwan Swaminarayan describes his own principle. If God is pleased with him and he has the company of devotees, he would feel no grief even if far from God. A person with God's pleasure and the company of devotees, he says, is already in the abode of God while on earth. His resolution was simply to serve God's devotees.

The book turns this into a practical habit. Before an action, ask: will this please them? During it: are they pleased? Afterwards: were they pleased, and could it be even better? This turns ordinary tasks, an email, a phone call or a conversation, into a quiet offering. Nothing needs to be grand for it to count.
teachings.quote: even though he is in Mrutyulok, he is still in the abode of God
teachings.ch: Ch. 1, "Swaminarayan Sadhana", pp. 18-20; Ch. 14, "Satatya: Continuity", p. 257
teachings.take: Before one task today, pause and ask: 'Will this please Maharaj and Swami?'
reflects: What does rajipo mean to you, in your own words?
Which part of your day could become an offering?
How does it feel to know God's abode can be felt here, among devotees?
Whose company helps you feel that God is pleased?
What task might you do differently if you asked 'will this please him?'
How is seeking God's pleasure different from seeking people's approval?
When have you felt that Maharaj was pleased with you?
What small act of service could you offer a devotee this week?
How could you check in gently with yourself after a task?
What would a day lived for his rajipo look like?
teachings.reflect: What does rajipo mean to you, in your own words?

teachings.title: Only through your wish
parts: Bhagatji Maharaj, also known as Pragji Bhakta, is the second guru in the Gunatit succession after Bhagwan Swaminarayan. The book describes how he spent thirteen years closely associated with Gopalanand Swami, serving him and listening to his talks. Gopalanand Swami then sent him to Gunatitanand Swami to receive true spiritual knowledge.

He went on to give years of wholehearted service to Gunatitanand Swami, taking every word of his guru to heart and letting none go to waste. At the end of this, Gunatitanand Swami was deeply pleased and blessed him with the realisation of Bhagwan Swaminarayan. Bhagatji Maharaj's response was not pride. It was wonder.

He prayed that great sages had endured far more and performed far greater practices, yet he had been given the bliss of Akshardham, God's divine abode, and could only conclude it came through God's wish. The book points out that after all his effort, he still counted it as nothing beside what he had been given. Grace, not scorekeeping, was his conclusion.
teachings.quote: I realize that I have received this bliss only through your wish.
teachings.take: Tonight, name one good thing in your life and say: 'This came through your wish.'
reflects: What in your life feels like a gift you did not earn?
How does Bhagatji Maharaj's humility speak to you?
When do you find yourself keeping score with God?
What would it feel like to see your blessings as his wish?
Who has guided you patiently, as Gopalanand Swami guided Bhagatji Maharaj?
What effort of yours are you proud of, and could you offer it to him?
How does gratitude change the way you see your own hard work?
What is one grace you noticed this week?
How might you thank God for something without using words?
What would you like to receive 'only through his wish' in the coming year?
teachings.reflect: What in your life feels like a gift you did not earn?

teachings.title: The bhakti that suits you
parts: The book lists many forms of bhakti: listening, singing, remembering, serving, worshipping, bowing, being a servant, friendship with God and total surrender. Reading about them all, it admits, a person might reasonably ask: do I have to do all of this every day? How will I manage anything else in my life?

Its answer is kind. A patient does not take every medicine in the pharmacy, only what suits their condition. Likewise, in Vachanamrut Gadhada III 14 and 15, Bhagwan Swaminarayan teaches that whichever of the nine forms of bhakti best fixes your mind on God is the best one for you. Recognise it as your own inclination and keep it at the centre.

The other forms still support you, but you do not need to squeeze yourself into a shape that is not yours. Some people come alive in kirtan, some in quiet remembrance, some in seva. Noticing which form draws you closest to God is the very first step Maharaj describes. Your path may look different from others'.
teachings.quote: whichever type aids one in developing firm attachment to God is the best
teachings.take: Notice which moment of devotion today felt most alive, and give it a little more time tomorrow.
reflects: Which form of bhakti feels most natural to you?
When does your mind settle most easily on God?
Is there a form of devotion you have been forcing yourself into?
How does it feel to hear that you do not need to do everything?
Which form of bhakti did you love as a child?
What would a day built around your favourite form look like?
How might your inclination change in different seasons of life?
Who do you know whose bhakti looks different from yours?
What helps you notice when you feel close to God?
What is one way to give your favourite form more space this week?
teachings.reflect: Which form of bhakti feels most natural to you?

teachings.title: Puja without a single item
parts: Mansi puja means worship offered in the mind. Instead of physical flowers or a murti in front of you, you picture God and lovingly offer everything mentally. In Vachanamrut Gadhada III 23, Bhagwan Swaminarayan says a devotee performs mansi puja of God daily, and even suggests varying it with the seasons of summer, winter and monsoon.

The book describes the tradition, followed since Maharaj's time, of five mansis through the day. In the morning you imagine gently waking Maharaj, bathing and dressing him, offering garlands and arti, the waving of lights. Further mansis follow at midday, late afternoon and evening, and at night you picture him resting comfortably as you massage his feet.

Its great beauty, the book notes, is that it needs no items, no murti and no particular place. Nothing about time, age, wealth or circumstance can stop it. It can be done on a bus, in a waiting room or lying awake at night, simply by focusing on the murti that lives in your heart.
teachings.quote: One who is a devotee of God daily performs the mansi puja of God.
teachings.take: Tonight before sleeping, picture Maharaj resting and gently offer him a garland in your mind.
reflects: Have you ever tried mansi puja? What was it like?
Which of the five mansis would suit your day best?
What would you most like to offer Maharaj in your mind?
Where could you do a quiet mansi during the week?
How does it feel to know worship needs no items at all?
Which details of Maharaj's murti do you picture most easily?
How might mansi help on days when you cannot get to the mandir?
What seasonal offering would you imagine right now?
How does picturing Maharaj resting make you feel?
Who could you share this practice with?
teachings.reflect: Have you ever tried mansi puja? What was it like?

teachings.title: Where Shri Hari lives
parts: Dasya bhakti is devotion offered as a servant. The book quotes Bhagwan Swaminarayan's description from the Shrihari Charitramrut Sagar, a scripture of his life and teachings: letting go of ego, behaving as God's servant and being on time for seva. Such a person, whatever their status, feels fortunate to do even the humblest seva, like sweeping the mandir.

Hanumanji is the book's great example of this devotion, serving Shri Ram with total humility and loyalty. Maharaj also describes the true servant as someone who stays humble with everyone, respects others as higher than themselves, and is never deceitful. It is a posture of the heart more than a list of jobs.

In another line he says that without servitude, even mountains of virtue do not shine; they are like zeros with no one in front. Then comes a beautiful promise: Shri Hari, God, resides in the heart of a servant. Humility is not the same as smallness. It is making room for God to live in you.
teachings.quote: Shri Hari resides in the heart of a servant
teachings.take: Do one small, unseen task for someone today without mentioning it.
reflects: What does being a 'servant of God' mean to you?
Which humble seva do you quietly enjoy?
What do you admire most in Hanumanji's devotion?
When is it hardest for you to treat others as higher than yourself?
In your experience, how does humility make room for God?
Who do you know who serves without needing recognition?
What small, unseen task could you do this week?
How do you feel when your help goes unnoticed?
What would change if you saw every task as seva?
Where would you like Shri Hari to feel at home in you?
teachings.reflect: What does being a 'servant of God' mean to you?

teachings.title: Seva is a mirror
parts: Many spiritual practices are done alone: meditation, reading, chanting. The book makes an honest observation about them. On your own, there is no one to clash with, so ego, jealousy or impatience can lie hidden, untouched and unnoticed. You may never discover they are there. Practising alone has great value, but it cannot show you everything.

Seva is different. Working alongside others, opinions differ, plans change and patience is tested. That is exactly what makes it so valuable, because it shows you what is really inside. The book quotes Bhagwan Swaminarayan from the Shrihari Charitramrut Sagar: there is no test equal to seva, and it is the root of all other practices.

The book also suggests an attitude to bring with you: thinking that it is your great good fortune to be given this chance to serve, and asking what you can do for others rather than what they will do for you. Seen this way, a tricky moment in seva is not a failure but a mirror, gently showing what you are ready to work on.
teachings.quote: There is no test equivalent to seva.
teachings.take: In your next group task, notice one feeling that rises in you, and meet it kindly.
reflects: Which of your traits shows up most when working with others?
What has seva taught you about yourself?
When did a disagreement in seva help you grow?
How do you usually react when plans change at the last minute?
How does 'it is my good fortune to serve' feel to say?
Who have you enjoyed doing seva alongside, and why?
What would you like seva to help you work on?
How can you be kind to yourself when seva shows you a flaw?
What small seva could you offer in your home this week?
How is serving with others different from praying alone, for you?
teachings.reflect: Which of your traits shows up most when working with others?

teachings.title: Stones for the mandir
parts: The book gathers a series of scenes. Bhagwan Swaminarayan himself carried stones for the building of the mandir in Gadhada. Gunatitanand Swami engaged Pragji Bhakta, who had come to him seeking spiritual knowledge, in preparing lime and mortar and carrying heavy stones for the work at Junagadh mandir. Even those who came for wisdom were first handed humble work.

Shastriji Maharaj involved devotees in building mandirs, and Yogiji Maharaj had young people gather stones on the farm and clean toilets and bathrooms. Pramukh Swami Maharaj, reflecting on all this, observed that none of them had simply sat in intense meditation. Meditation has its place, he said, but seva done as the guru wishes is most important.

He also explained why. Doing only meditation, he said, can increase ego and laziness, while seva brings happiness and inspires others. There is something grounding in this. When the mind feels heavy, putting your hands to a useful task for others is not a distraction from devotion. For the gurus, it was devotion.
teachings.quote: No one has simply sat in intense meditation.
teachings.take: Offer your hands to one practical task at home or at the mandir this week, as seva.
reflects: Which of these scenes of the gurus doing seva moves you most?
What practical seva do you find most satisfying?
How do you feel after doing something useful for others?
When has working with your hands helped a heavy mind?
What seva could you offer at the mandir or at home?

How can you balance quiet prayer with active seva?
Who has inspired you through their seva?
What would you like to build, in any sense, for others?
What does 'seva as devotion' mean in your daily life?
teachings.reflect: Which of these scenes of the gurus doing seva moves you most?

teachings.title: Even ringing a bell
parts: Agna means a command or instruction from God or the guru, and anuvrutti means sensing and following their inner wishes. The book describes following both as a special form of bhakti. It includes daily observances such as puja, arti and listening to discourses, as well as occasional requests the guru makes.

Yogiji Maharaj said something striking about how much even small acts can matter. Ringing a bell because the Satpurush, the God-realised guru, wished it is described, he said, as behaving as the atma, the soul. For him, spiritual maturity meant not letting any instruction lapse, whether it was small or big.

This is encouraging for days when you cannot do much. You do not need a grand gesture to be spiritually alive. Doing your daily puja, joining the arti, going to the weekly assembly: small acts done because the guru wished them carry real spiritual meaning, and every one of them counts.
teachings.quote: Even ringing a bell by the wish of the Satpurush
teachings.take: Choose one small daily niyam (observance), like arti or puja, and do it today with full attention.
reflects: Which small daily practice feels most meaningful to you?
How does it feel to know small acts can carry real spiritual meaning?

Which one would you like to follow more wholeheartedly?
When has a tiny act of devotion lifted your day?
How can you bring full attention to something simple?
If you could ring one bell for the guru today, what would it be for?
Who in your life follows small instructions with great love?
What gets in the way of your small daily practices?
What is one small thing you could offer with joy tomorrow?
teachings.reflect: Which small daily practice feels most meaningful to you?

teachings.title: The neem tree at Junagadh
parts: Someone once asked Gunatitanand Swami why a devotee might drift away from satsang even after becoming close to the guru. His answer, recorded in the Swamini Vato, came with a tree. When the mandir at Junagadh was being built, he said, a neem tree there was only two hands tall. A single person could have pulled it out.

But now, he went on, even if everyone in the village came together, they could not uproot it. In the same way, he explained, when a person's bond with satsang has grown strong over many days, it is no longer shaken by temptations or by the restless desires that come and go.

The image is hopeful. Faith does not need to be huge from the start. It grows the way a tree does: slowly, quietly, one season after another, until its roots run deep. Each visit to the mandir, each conversation with devotees, each prayer is a little more root beneath the soil.
teachings.quote: even if all these people of the village get together they cannot uproot it
teachings.ch: Ch. 13, "Satpurushno Prasang: Association of the Satpurush", p. 226
teachings.take: Add one small root today: a message to a satsangi friend, a darshan, or one prayer.
reflects: How tall would you say your 'neem tree' of faith is right now?
What has helped your roots grow deeper over the years?
When did you feel your faith was easily shaken?
What small habits water your faith week by week?

What storms has your faith already come through?
What would help your roots this month?
How can you be patient with a young faith, yours or someone else's?
What does a deeply rooted faith look like to you?
teachings.reflect: How tall would you say your 'neem tree' of faith is right now?

teachings.title: Sugar in milk
parts: Yogiji Maharaj used a homely image to describe closeness to God and the guru. Oil and water can sit in the same glass yet stay separate. In the same way, he said, a person can live near God and the Sant while their mind stays disconnected. Instead, he said, we should be like sugar and milk, which merge completely.

The book develops this. Sugar dissolved in water separates again when the water boils away. Sugar dissolved in milk does not; however long it is heated, the sugar never leaves. Sang, ordinary association, is like sugar in water. Prasang, a deep and lasting bond with the guru, is like sugar in milk.

The book adds that over ninety per cent of this bond is formed in the mind: remembering the guru's virtues, recalling incidents from his life, praying to him and being open with him. It is less about how often you are physically near him, and more about how fully your heart is joined to his.
teachings.quote: We should live like sugar and milk which completely merge with one another.
teachings.ch: Ch. 13, "Satpurushno Prasang: Association of the Satpurush", pp. 227-232
teachings.take: Recall one moment from the guru's life today and let it sit quietly in your heart.
reflects: Does your connection with the guru feel more like water or milk right now?
What helps your heart feel joined, not just nearby?
Which memory of the guru do you return to most?

What kinds of 'heat' test a relationship with God?

How could you be more open with God in prayer?
Which virtue of the guru would you most like to absorb?
When have you felt close to the guru without being physically near?
What would help your bond grow deeper this month?
teachings.reflect: Does your connection with the guru feel more like water or milk right now?

teachings.title: Hearing it for the first time
parts: The Swamini Vato records a lovely moment. A devotee read five Vachanamruts aloud to Gunatitanand Swami. When he finished, Swami sat up and said it was as if he had never heard these Vachanamruts before, and asked for them to be read again. So the devotee read them all a second time.

Gunatitanand Swami knew Bhagwan Swaminarayan's words intimately, yet he listened as if for the very first time. After the second reading he reflected that the teachings made it clear there was no alternative but to live by them, for anyone at all, however great their position. Familiarity had not dulled his attention; if anything, it deepened his listening.

The book elsewhere describes listening as an art with three parts: listening with full concentration, manan (reflecting on what you heard and what to keep) and nididhyas (recalling it again and again through the day). A familiar passage can still surprise you if you meet it with fresh ears. Hearing it again is not repetition.
teachings.quote: It is as if I had never heard these Vachanamruts.
teachings.ch: Ch. 8, "Swadharmanishtha: Jnan", p. 122; Ch. 5, "Swadharmanishtha: Bhakti I", pp. 76-78
teachings.take: Reread one familiar Vachanamrut today as if for the first time, and note one new line.
reflects: Which teaching have you heard so often that you stopped really hearing it?

What helps you listen with full attention?

How could you reflect on a teaching after hearing it?

What does 'fresh ears' mean for you in satsang?
teachings.reflect: Which teaching have you heard so often that you stopped really hearing it?

teachings.title: Jala Bhakta's missing piece
parts: In one of Gunatitanand Swami's recorded talks, someone asked a sincere question. Satsang teaches that a person can become brahmarup, sharing the qualities of Brahman, so why does it not happen? Swami answered that the person has not attached themselves to the guru with love, and even when they have, they do not fully trust him.

He then gave a real example, pointing to a devotee called Jala Bhakta who had firmly attached his jiva, his soul, to Swami but did not trust him. Swami went on to say that there may even be trust, yet a person does not honestly open up. If one is completely honest, he said, the change cannot fail to happen.

In a related talk he adds that the guru's virtues come to those who see him as free of faults and all-knowing, and who are frank with him. It is a gentle invitation. You do not need to hide your struggles from God or the guru. Openness itself is part of the path.
teachings.quote: This Jala Bhakta has firmly attached his jiva to me but does not trust me.
teachings.ch: Ch. 13, "Satpurushno Prasang: Association of the Satpurush", pp. 223-224
teachings.take: In prayer tonight, tell Maharaj one thing honestly that you usually keep to yourself.
reflects: What do you find hardest to be honest about in prayer?

teachings.reflect: What do you find hardest to be honest about in prayer?

teachings.title: The one principle
parts: Divyabhav means perceiving divinity: understanding God and the guru as wholly divine, even in their human-like actions. The book presents this as one of the most important forms of bhakti, and calls it the true sadhana of an aspirant. Yogiji Maharaj spoke about it with disarming simplicity. He did not make it complicated at all.

He said that in fifty years of satsang, the one thing he had learnt from the great sadgurus was to perceive divinity, and that this is the single principle running through all the Vachanamruts. He widened it beyond the guru, too, asking devotees to see the whole community of devotees, which he called the Gunatit garden, as divine.

The book treats this as something that grows by degrees, strengthened by prayer, trust in the shastras and stories of devotees who kept their faith in difficult times. It also brings a quiet peace. When you look for the divine in the guru and in those around you, there is less room for agitation inside.
teachings.quote: The one principle of all the Vachanamruts is to perceive divinity.
teachings.take: Look for one divine quality in someone at the mandir or at home today.
reflects: What does seeing divinity in the guru mean to you?
