teachings.reflect: What does seeing divinity in the guru mean to you?

teachings.title: Five Ms for family life
parts: In its chapter on unity, the book offers five simple words, all beginning with M, for keeping relationships warm and strong. They apply to a family, a satsang group or anywhere people live and work together. None of them is complicated, but together they form a quiet habit of care.

Mahima means appreciating the greatness of others, especially fellow devotees. Mamta means love, treating others as your own. Madad means help, in whatever way you can; if nothing else is possible, you can at least pray for them. Milan means meeting: asking after each other's wellbeing, talking about spiritual things, and for households, holding ghar sabha, a family assembly at home.

Mafi means forgiveness: forgiving others their mistakes, and setting ego aside to ask forgiveness when you are the one who has erred. None of these needs a grand gesture. A kind word, a short prayer, a phone call or a sincere sorry can each keep a relationship warm. Small and often is what matters.
teachings.quote: If nothing else is possible, at least prayers can be offered.
teachings.take: Pick one M today: send a caring message, offer help, or say a quiet prayer for someone.
reflects: Which of the five Ms comes most naturally to you?
Which one would you like to practise more?
Who in your family could use a little madad this week?

teachings.reflect: Which of the five Ms comes most naturally to you?

teachings.title: Highlight the one virtue
parts: Suhrudbhav means a friendly spirit towards everyone, a genuine wish for others' wellbeing. Yogiji Maharaj explained it through a handful of short sayings recorded in the book. Each one is practical, easy to remember and just a little challenging, the kind of line that follows you into ordinary conversations. They are easy to carry with you through a busy day.

One of them is this: suhrudbhav is to overlook the faults of others, and even if a person has a hundred faults, to highlight their one virtue. In another saying he describes it as seeing even the smallest devotee as greater than ourselves, as servants of servants. Both sayings turn our usual habit of noticing faults completely around.

This is not about pretending faults do not exist. It is about choosing where your attention rests. The book records Pramukh Swami Maharaj saying that there is only unrest in dwelling on the faults of others. Searching for the one good thing in someone who frustrates you can soften both of you.
teachings.quote: Despite a person's 100 faults, highlight his one virtue.
teachings.ch: Ch. 10, "Sampnishtha: Unity", p. 156; Ch. 12, "Savdhani: Kusang", p. 202
teachings.take: Think of someone who frustrates you and name, silently, one genuine virtue they have.
reflects: Whose one virtue could you focus on this week?
What happens inside you when you dwell on someone's faults?

How easy is it for you to see yourself as a 'servant of servants'?

How might highlighting a virtue change a tense conversation?
When have you been surprised by someone's goodness?
What would suhrudbhav look like in your home?
How can you be as generous with yourself as with others?
Which relationship would benefit from a friendlier spirit?
teachings.reflect: Whose one virtue could you focus on this week?

teachings.title: Every aspirant is a patient
parts: After many pages on avoiding fault-finding, the book lists some realities to accept, and they are refreshingly humane. People will have flaws until they are fully transformed. Nobody comes to satsang already free of their faults; they come in order to work on them. In satsang, the book says, every aspirant is a patient.

It goes on: changing a habit or nature is not as quick as we assume, and the time it takes is not the same for everyone. If it is hard for you to change, it is hard for others too. No one can remove another person's faults by talking about them, and everyone's path will look different.

Finally, it reminds us that transforming each person is the work of Maharaj and the guru, in their own way and time, not ours. This brings two kinds of relief: patience with others, and patience with yourself. You are a patient too, and patients are there to be cared for.
teachings.quote: In Satsang, every aspirant is a patient.
teachings.take: When someone's habit annoys you today, think: 'We are both patients here.'
reflects: How does it feel to think of everyone in satsang as a patient?
Which of your own habits has been slowest to change?
Whose slow change could you be more patient with?
What relief comes from knowing transformation is Maharaj's work?
When have you tried to fix someone else, and how did it go?
How would you treat yourself if you were your own patient?
What does progress look like for you, even when it is slow?
Who has been patient with you while you grew?
How could this idea change the way you see family members?
What would you like to leave in Maharaj's hands today?
teachings.reflect: How does it feel to think of everyone in satsang as a patient?

teachings.title: The frozen well
parts: Bhagatji Maharaj once explained inner steadiness to a sadhu, Pavitranand Swami, with a simple picture. Throw a small pebble into a well and ripples spread across the water. But if the water in the well is frozen, the pebble simply bounces off and no ripples form at all. It is an image anyone can picture instantly.

Our minds, he said, may seem calm to us, but when we are praised or insulted, ripples of thought rise up. Through close association with the Gunatit guru, the mind can become like the frozen well, so that such moments bounce off and do not disturb us inside. With love for Maharaj, he added, fountains of joy would burst forth.

In that state, he said, all words would be considered nothing more than a part of space. Harsh comments, careless remarks and even praise would lose their grip. For anyone who replays conversations or takes words deeply to heart, this is a hopeful image of a mind that can grow steadier over time.
teachings.quote: all words will be considered nothing more than a part of space
teachings.take: When a comment stings today, picture it as a pebble bouncing off still ice.
reflects: Whose words tend to ripple through you the longest?
Does praise or criticism affect you more?
What helps your mind settle after a hurtful comment?
How might a closer bond with the guru steady you?
When have you let something go more easily than you expected?
What does 'words are part of space' mean to you?
Which conversation do you tend to replay, and why?
How could you respond to your own ripples with kindness?
Who do you know who stays calm under criticism?
What would a 'frozen well' day look like for you?
teachings.reflect: Whose words tend to ripple through you the longest?

teachings.title: What would Swami do here?
parts: The book offers a very practical way to grow closer to the guru: carry him into your ordinary moments. Written while Pramukh Swami Maharaj was guru, it suggests that during any action we ask what Pramukh Swami Maharaj would do if he were in our place, and how he would have done it.

It goes further. Would his actions carry ill feeling, jealousy, ego or malice? Has he ever looked for faults in anyone? Reflecting on the incidents of his life, the book says, the answer is always no. By asking these questions again and again, we gradually take on something of his nature.

This is a small, portable practice. Before replying to a sharp message, before a difficult conversation at home, before walking into an interview, you can pause and picture the guru in your place. His calm, patience and kindness become a guide you can consult anywhere, at any moment. It needs no preparation and no special place.
teachings.quote: What would Pramukh Swami Maharaj do if he was in my place?
teachings.take: Before one tricky moment today, pause and ask: 'What would Swami do here?'
reflects: In which situation today would this question help you most?
What do you imagine the guru would do differently from you?
Which quality of the guru would you most like to borrow?
When have you acted as you imagine he would?
How might this question change a family disagreement?
What would the guru say about how you treat yourself?
How do you picture him walking into a job interview?
Which incident from his life helps you picture his response?
What makes it hard to pause before reacting?
How could you remind yourself to ask this question?
teachings.reflect: In which situation today would this question help you most?

teachings.title: The mango sapling
parts: Gunatitanand Swami once described how listening to spiritual talks can transform a person completely, changing how they see everything around them. Then he voiced the obvious objection his listeners might raise: if we keep listening to these talks, why has nothing like this happened to us yet? It is a question many sincere people quietly ask themselves.

His reply was a picture from the orchard. If you plant a mango sapling today, how could it give mangoes by tomorrow? But ten years later, that same tree will give mangoes. This, he said, is simply how it happens. The planting is real, even when there is no fruit to show for it.

The same is true of so much that matters: healing, habits, skills and the search for good work. Effort sown today may show nothing for a long while. That quiet stretch is not failure; it is growing time. You are allowed to keep watering a tree that has not fruited yet.
teachings.quote: if you plant a mango sapling today, how can mangoes grow by tomorrow?
teachings.take: Name one 'sapling' you are tending right now, and water it with one small action today.
reflects: What sapling are you tending at the moment?
Where are you expecting fruit sooner than is fair?
How does the image of a ten-year tree make you feel?
What small action could water your efforts today?
When has patience paid off for you in the past?
Who in your life has grown something slowly and well?
How can you tell growth is happening when nothing shows yet?
What would you say to a friend who was waiting for results?
What helps you keep going when there is no visible progress?
What fruit do you hope to see in a year's time?
teachings.reflect: What sapling are you tending at the moment?

teachings.title: The soft rope and the stone
parts: At the edge of an old well sits a stone. A soft rope is pulled across it day after day to draw water. Over a long time, that soft rope wears a groove into the hard stone. Bhagwan Swaminarayan uses this image in Vachanamrut Gadhada II 1, noting that even an iron chain would not cut such a groove quickly.

His point is that deep change cannot be achieved in a single day, or in a hurry. It comes to those who work at it gradually and earnestly. He then adds, strikingly, that those striving should not become frustrated or upset. One can think: I will do as much as is possible in this life, and keep courage while persevering.

The gentleness is the lesson. You do not have to be the iron chain, forcing results. You can be the soft rope, returning each day with the same small effort. Whether it is a routine, a new skill or a job search, steady and kind persistence shapes what force cannot.
teachings.quote: They should not become frustrated or upset.
teachings.take: Choose one small daily effort and repeat it gently today, without judging the result.
reflects: Where are you trying to be an iron chain instead of a soft rope?
What small effort could you repeat every day this week?
How does Maharaj's advice not to be frustrated feel to you?
What groove would you like your daily efforts to wear?
When has gentle persistence worked for you before?
Which part of your routine feels most like the soft rope?
How can you measure progress without being harsh?
What would 'as much as is possible' look like for you today?
Who encourages your steady efforts?
What do you need to stop rushing?
teachings.reflect: Where are you trying to be an iron chain instead of a soft rope?

teachings.title: Not sitting idly
parts: When you are between jobs, or unable to do as much as you would like, it is easy to feel you are wasting time. Days can seem empty if they do not produce something you can point to. Gunatitanand Swami said something in the Swamini Vato that gently challenges that feeling.

When we set aside all other work and become free to listen to spiritual talks, he said, we should understand that we are doing tens of millions of tasks, because through these talks the soul's heaviest burdens are being lifted. Then he added a line that speaks to anyone who feels unproductive: do not think we are sitting idly.

Time spent in katha, reading the Vachanamrut, or quietly listening to a spiritual talk is not empty time. It is unseen work, and in his eyes very important work. On a day when the job search stalls, an hour given to satsang is still an hour well spent. It is part of the real work of your life.
teachings.quote: But do not think we are sitting idly.
teachings.take: Give twenty minutes today to a katha or reading, and count it as real work done.
reflects: When do you feel most unproductive, and what do you tell yourself then?
How does it feel to hear that listening to satsang is not idleness?
Which spiritual talk or reading has helped you recently?
How could you build a short katha into your weekday?
What counts as 'real work' to you, and could that widen?
Who reminds you that your time has value?
What unseen work is happening in you at the moment?
How can you rest from striving without feeling bad about it?
Which Swamini Vato or Vachanamrut would you like to read next?
What would a balanced day of effort and satsang look like?
teachings.reflect: When do you feel most unproductive, and what do you tell yourself then?

teachings.title: A goal that steadies you
parts: Sankalpnishtha means firm commitment to a goal. The book opens its chapter on it with an everyday observation: much of what people achieve comes from clarity about what they want and conviction in it. Without that clarity, the first real obstacle can be enough to make us give up. A clear aim gives us something to hold on to.

It lists the fruits of a clear goal. Time and energy are organised rather than scattered. Priorities become clear. Life becomes more ordered and consistent. Faith, patience and enthusiasm grow. And, perhaps most comforting of all, one stays steady through difficulty and failure, and will somehow find a way to keep moving forward.

The book's highest goal is spiritual: to please God and the guru and become brahmarup. But its ways of strengthening a goal suit any aim: write your thoughts down daily, read them aloud, reflect on them, talk them over with good company and pray for strength. Clarity is built, not simply found.
teachings.quote: One will somehow find a way to keep moving forward.
teachings.take: Write one sentence about what you are aiming for this month, and read it aloud tonight.
reflects: What is one goal that matters deeply to you right now?
How clear does that goal feel, on a scale of one to ten?
What pulls your time and energy in too many directions?
How might writing your goal down each day help?
Who could you talk your goals over with?
What is your deepest spiritual aim, in your own words?
How do your work goals and spiritual goals fit together?
When has a clear aim helped you through a setback?
What prayer would strengthen your resolve?
What is one step forward you can take this week?
teachings.reflect: What is one goal that matters deeply to you right now?

teachings.title: Of course I can
parts: The book includes guidance, drawn from the lives of Bhagwan Swaminarayan and the gurus, on how to follow the instructions of God and the guru. Much of it is simple and very human: do not delay, carry out the task with joy rather than anxiety, and follow it with faith, patience and perseverance.

One line stands out. However difficult the task, do not begin by telling yourself it is beyond you. Instead, tell yourself that of course you can manage it, and ask why you would not be able to. Then simply do it. The book adds: be precise, systematic and regular, and do not let boredom creep in.

It also advises working cooperatively, in friendship and teamwork, and staying steady through praise and criticism, success and failure. For anyone preparing applications or facing interviews, this is a helpful inner script: not arrogance, but a quiet confidence that with God's strength the next step is possible. Each small step is enough for today.
teachings.quote: why would I not be able to?
teachings.take: Before one daunting task today, say: 'With Maharaj's strength, why would I not be able to?'
reflects: Which task have you been telling yourself you cannot do?
What would change if you asked 'why would I not be able to?'
When have you surprised yourself by managing something hard?
How does faith give you confidence without arrogance?
What is one small step you could take on a daunting task today?
Who believes in you more than you believe in yourself?
How do you usually talk to yourself before an interview?
What does staying steady through success and failure mean to you?
How could teamwork make a hard task easier?
What would you attempt if you trusted God's strength a little more?
teachings.reflect: Which task have you been telling yourself you cannot do?

teachings.title: Five realities, one map
parts: Bhagwan Swaminarayan taught that five realities, called tattvas, exist eternally: Parabrahman (God, also called Purushottam), Aksharbrahman (Akshar, God's abode and ideal devotee), ishwars (powerful beings such as the deities who govern creation), jivas (individual souls, like you and me) and maya (the material energy from which the universe is made). None of them was ever created and none will ever be destroyed.

These five are never blurred into one another. Each keeps its own nature in every state, whether the universe is being created, sustained or dissolved, and whether a soul is bound or liberated. Four of them are conscious; maya alone is not. Maharaj said he formed this principle from the Vedas, Purans, Itihas and Smrutis, so it is rooted in the wider scriptures, not invented.

The book explains how they relate with two words: sharir and shariri, the body and the one who dwells in it. Just as you live in and move your body, Parabrahman dwells within the other four as their supporter, controller and inspirer, while staying untouched by their flaws. Everything depends on him; he depends on nothing. Every other teaching sits on this map.
teachings.quote: jiva, maya, ishwar, Brahman and Parabrahman are all eternal
teachings.take: When you pray today, picture yourself as one small jiva, held and supported by Parabrahman.
reflects: Which of the five tattvas did you understand least before reading this?
How does it feel to know your jiva was never created and will never end?
What in your life feels held up by something bigger than you?
Where do you notice God as your inner support on an ordinary day?
Which idea here would you most like to explain to a friend?
What question would you ask a sadhu about the five tattvas?
How might remembering that everything depends on God ease one worry you have now?
What is one thing you rely on today that ultimately rests on Him?
When did you last feel supported without having to ask for it?
How would you describe the word 'indweller' in your own words?
teachings.reflect: Which of the five tattvas did you understand least before reading this?

teachings.title: Not lost like a river
parts: Some traditions picture liberation as a river flowing into the sea and disappearing, or a small light merging into a bigger one. Bhagwan Swaminarayan taught differently. A liberated soul becomes an akshar-mukta (a freed soul in Akshardham) and keeps its own individual existence for ever. It never dissolves into Aksharbrahman or Parabrahman (Vachanamrut G II 38, G III 33).

The liberated soul receives a radiant, divine form like God's and remains near him in Akshardham. The bond between the one who worships and the One who is worshipped never ends. The book adds a lovely detail: in Akshardham there is no other work to be done, because simply having God's darshan is the service. The muktas are so absorbed in his bliss that they forget themselves.

So the goal of satsang is not the end of you. It is you, fully yourself and finally free, in a relationship of love with Maharaj that never runs out. Every small act of devotion you offer now, every prayer and every moment of darshan, belongs to a story in which you remain, and in which that love only deepens.
teachings.quote: the darshan of God is itself the service
teachings.ch: Ch. 15, "Mukti Mimansa: Deep Reflection on Liberation", pp. 203-204; Ch. 1, pp. 8-9
teachings.take: Offer one small act of devotion today as yourself, knowing that 'you' will never be lost.
reflects: What did you imagine liberation looked like before reading this?
How does it feel to know your individuality is eternal?
What part of your relationship with Maharaj would you most like to keep for ever?
When have you felt absorbed in darshan, even briefly?
What would it mean for darshan itself to be your seva today?
Which quality of yours do you hope God enjoys?
How does this change the way you think about who you are?
What small act of devotion feels most natural to you right now?
Who in your life helped you feel you are worth keeping?
What would you say to Maharaj if you had one moment of darshan today?
teachings.reflect: What did you imagine liberation looked like before reading this?

teachings.title: Like the waxing moon
parts: In Vachanamrut Vartal 12, Bhagwan Swaminarayan describes how faith grows. Before a soul develops conviction in God, he says, it is as dim as the moon on Amas, the new moon night, with no more light than a glow-worm. Then, through close association with the Sant (a God-realised sadhu), it begins to brighten.

It grows like the moon from the second night of the bright fortnight. Each night a little more is lit, until at Punam, the full moon, it shines completely. Maharaj says that when faith is joined with understanding of God's greatness, even one's own mind and senses can no longer shake it, and such a devotee becomes fearless.

The moon does not jump from dark to full overnight, and it is no less the moon on the third night than on the fifteenth. Faith is allowed to grow slowly. If today feels more like a thin crescent than a full moon, it is still growing, night by night.
teachings.quote: progresses spiritually day by day, just like the waxing moon
teachings.take: Tonight, look for the moon if you can and notice how much of it is lit.
reflects: If your faith were a phase of the moon today, which would it be?
What helped your faith grow a little brighter this month?
When have you felt closest to the full moon of Punam?
What kind of association with the Sant helps you most?
How can you be patient with a slow-growing faith?
What small sign tells you something in you is brightening?
Who has been like the sun for your moon?
What would a fearless devotee do differently in your situation?
Which doubt would you like steadier faith to settle?
What would you tell a friend who felt their faith was only a crescent?
teachings.reflect: If your faith were a phase of the moon today, which would it be?

teachings.title: An ocean of virtues
parts: The book explains that Parabrahman is both sagun and nirgun, which sounds contradictory until you learn what the words mean here. Sagun means he possesses countless divine, uplifting qualities. Nirgun means he has none of maya's worldly qualities: no anger, greed, jealousy, pride or ego, and nothing mundane in his form (Vachanamrut G I 66).

Among his qualities Maharaj lists daya (compassion), kshama (forgiveness), vatsalya (a parent's affection), saulabhya (being easy to reach), dhairya (patience) and madhurya (sweetness), and many more (G I 62, G II 67). That is why he is called gunsagar, an ocean of virtues. The book stresses these are not poetic exaggerations; they are real and eternal parts of who he is.

Pause on saulabhya and vatsalya in particular. The One who controls infinite universes is also, by his very nature, easy to approach and tender like a parent. You do not have to earn an appointment or find the perfect words. When you turn to him, you turn to someone whose forgiveness and patience never run low.
teachings.quote: Such virtues are a natural part of God; they are real.
teachings.take: Pick one of God's qualities from this list and name it to Him in your prayer tonight.
reflects: Which of God's virtues listed here touches you most today?
When have you felt God's patience with you?
What does 'easy to reach' mean to you in your prayers?
Which of these qualities do you most want to grow in yourself?
How does knowing God has no anger or jealousy change how you approach Him?
Where have you seen a parent's kind of affection in your own life?
What would you like to be forgiven for, and can you trust He already has?
Which virtue would help you most in your job search this week?
How might you show sweetness in one conversation today?
What surprised you about the meaning of sagun and nirgun?
teachings.reflect: Which of God's virtues listed here touches you most today?

teachings.title: A drop of water in His palm
parts: In Vachanamrut Gadhada II 53, Bhagwan Swaminarayan says that God sees every soul in countless universes as clearly as he sees a drop of water held in his palm. The book explains that this knowing is natural to him and complete: past, present and future, thoughts as well as words and actions.

That might sound daunting at first, but look at the picture Maharaj chose. A drop of water in someone's palm is close, held gently and in full view. It is not lost in a crowd or forgotten in a corner. The book adds that God knows the intentions behind every action, not only how things looked from the outside.

On days when you feel invisible or misunderstood, this is a quiet comfort. You do not have to explain yourself perfectly for God to understand. Even when others only see the result, he already sees what you meant, what you are carrying and how hard you are trying, and he holds all of it gently.
teachings.quote: as clearly as he sees a drop of water in his palm
teachings.take: When you feel unseen today, open your palm for a moment and remember you are held that clearly.
reflects: When did you last feel invisible or misunderstood?
What are you carrying right now that you have not told anyone?
How does it feel to know God sees your intentions, not just outcomes?
What effort of yours do you wish someone had noticed this week?
Is there something you would like to tell God, knowing He already understands?
How is being 'held in a palm' different from being watched?
Who in your life sees you most clearly, and how does that feel?
What good intention of yours did not turn out as planned recently?
How could you rest in being known today instead of explaining yourself?
What would you like God to see in you today?
teachings.reflect: When did you last feel invisible or misunderstood?

teachings.title: Dear, even if ordinary
parts: In Vachanamrut Gadhada I 37, Bhagwan Swaminarayan describes the devotee who is dear to him. It is not someone famous, gifted or extraordinarily austere. It is the one who understands that God alone is the all-doer, the one who does everything, so completely that not even a dry leaf can move without him.

Maharaj says such a person is dear to him even if they are an ordinary person, and that kal (time), karma and maya cannot exert their power over them. The book explains why: none of these forces act on their own. They can only do as much as God allows, just as ministers in a kingdom can act only as far as their king permits (G II 21).

So you do not need to become someone remarkable to be close to God. You need to trust that your life is in his hands, not at the mercy of chance, bad timing or fate. The book lists what this trust brings: peace of mind, love for God and a steadier heart. That trust itself is what makes an ordinary devotee dear.
teachings.quote: without God, even a dry leaf cannot be stirred
teachings.take: When something feels like bad luck today, gently correct the thought: 'This is in Maharaj's hands.'
reflects: Where do you tend to blame luck, timing or fate?
How does it feel to hear that an ordinary devotee is dear to Maharaj?
What part of your life feels most out of your control right now?
What would change if you believed that part was in God's hands?
Which 'minister', like time or circumstances, do you give too much power to?
When have you seen something work out that you could not have arranged?
What makes you feel you need to be remarkable to be loved?
How could you practise trusting God with one small outcome today?
Who is an ordinary devotee you admire, and why?
What does 'dear to God' mean to you personally?
teachings.reflect: Where do you tend to blame luck, timing or fate?

teachings.title: On an elephant or a donkey
parts: In Vachanamrut Gadhada I 74, Bhagwan Swaminarayan gives a vivid image. If God seats us on an elephant, a mark of honour, we should be happy there. If he seats us on a donkey, we should be just as happy. What matters is not the ride but staying attached to God's holy feet.

He says the same about bigger things: whether Satsang grows or shrinks, we should stay content, because everything happens by God's will. Like a dry leaf carried wherever the wind takes it, we can rest in his direction, remain dependent on him and keep worshipping joyfully, without letting frustration settle in the mind.

This is not a call to pretend everything is fine. It is an invitation to loosen your grip on how things should look. A job offer or a rejection, a bright day or a heavy one: you are still his, still on the journey, and still able to remember him on either ride.
teachings.quote: if he seats us on a donkey, then we should remain happy
teachings.take: Whatever today's ride is, say 'Your wish, Maharaj' once and keep going.
reflects: Does today feel more like an elephant or a donkey?
What outcome are you holding on to most tightly right now?
How could you stay attached to Maharaj whichever way it goes?
When has a 'donkey' season later turned out to hold something good?
What frustration would you like to set down today?
What does staying content look like for you, without pretending?
How might this image help you handle a job rejection?
What is one thing you can still do for God on a heavy day?
Who has shown you how to stay steady on either ride?
What would you say to Maharaj about the ride you are on now?
teachings.reflect: Does today feel more like an elephant or a donkey?

teachings.title: A form to love
parts: Many people think of God as a formless energy or a vast light. Bhagwan Swaminarayan taught clearly that Parabrahman eternally has a definite, divine form. It is not made of maya as our bodies are; it is radiant, human-like, serene and beautiful, and it resides in Akshardham (Vachanamrut G II 13, G III 38).

He gave reasons we can follow. Akash (space) is formless, so pots cannot be shaped from it; a world full of forms comes from a creator with form (G II 10). And where scripture describes God as a mass of light, that light must come from somewhere: it is the radiance of his form, as sunlight comes from the sun (G I 66).

Maharaj also spoke personally. He said that although he could constantly see that vast divine light, he was not drawn to it; he found deep bliss only in the darshan of God's form (L 14). A form can be seen, served and loved. That is why the murti in the mandir and in your puja is so precious.
teachings.quote: I experience profound bliss only from the darshan of God’s form.
teachings.take: During darshan or puja today, look at the murti's face for a few quiet breaths.
reflects: Did you ever picture God as formless light or energy?
How does believing God has a form change the way you pray?
Which murti do you feel most drawn to, and why?
What do you notice when you look at Maharaj's face in the murti?
Which of Maharaj's reasons for God having a form made most sense to you?
How is loving a form different from loving an idea?
What seva could you offer to the murti this week?
When has darshan brought you a moment of real joy?
How would you explain this teaching to a curious friend?
What would you like to say to Maharaj's murti today?
teachings.reflect: Did you ever picture God as formless light or energy?

teachings.title: Seated in one place, present everywhere
parts: How can God be in Akshardham and also everywhere? The book answers with two words. Vyatirek means transcendent: Parabrahman resides in Akshardham in his divine form. Anvay means immanent: through his antaryami (inner-dwelling) power he is present within everything and everyone, as their controller and witness (Vachanamrut G I 7, S 5).

Maharaj explained that when scriptures call God all-pervading, they do not mean he is formless like empty space. They mean he keeps his definite form in one place and yet, by his own power, gives darshan to all (V 13). He is within everything, yet like akash, which holds earth and water without being stained by them, he stays untouched by any flaw (K 8).

So God is not far away in a distant abode, out of reach. Nor is he a vague, impersonal force. He is a personal God, with a form you can picture and love, who is also right here within you, aware of you, and unaffected by whatever mess or heaviness surrounds you today.
teachings.quote: by using his own powers, he gives darshan to all while residing in one place
teachings.ch: Ch. 3, "Parabrahman: Attributes", p. 21; Ch. 5, pp. 44-45; Ch. 8, p. 121
teachings.take: Pause once today, hand on heart, and remember He is here as well as in Akshardham.
reflects: Do you usually think of God as far away or close by?
Where today would you like to remember that He is present?
How does it feel that God is within you but untouched by your struggles?
What mess or heaviness around you could you invite Him into?
When have you sensed God as a witness beside you?
Which word, anvay or vyatirek, speaks to you more today?
How could you remember His presence during a stressful task?
What difference does a personal God make compared with a vague force?
Where is one ordinary place you could greet Him this week?
What would you like the God within you to hear today?
teachings.reflect: Do you usually think of God as far away or close by?

teachings.title: The archer and the arrow
parts: Hindu scriptures describe many avatars, such as Ram and Krishna, who came to earth for particular tasks. Swaminarayan theology calls Parabrahman the avatari: the source from whom all avatars come. Someone once suggested to Gunatitanand Swami that the difference is like one actor playing many different roles. Swami gently disagreed and offered better pictures.

He said it is like the difference between a king and a nobleman, an archer and the arrow, the moon and the stars (Swamini Vato 6.33). The arrow does great work, but its power comes from the archer. The book explains that God enters those through whom avatars appear and works through them, as fire enters iron and makes it glow, while each remains distinct (Vachanamrut P 7).

This is taught with respect, not rivalry. The book notes that Maharaj never refuted any avatar or their devotees; he spoke of their glory. The point is to recognise who Bhagwan Swaminarayan is: the source from whom all that power flows, and the One we are blessed to have found.
teachings.quote: The difference between the avatars and their source is not like that.
teachings.take: When you see an avatar's murti, bow respectfully and remember the source of its power.
reflects: Had you heard the 'actor and roles' idea before? What did you think of it?
Which of Swami's comparisons helps you most: king, archer or moon?
How does the image of fire in iron help you understand this?
Why do you think Maharaj spoke of other avatars with respect?
How can you hold firm conviction while staying respectful of others' faith?
What does it mean to you that you have found the source itself?
How would you explain the avatari idea to a cousin in a sentence?
What question does this teaching raise for you?
Where in your life do you see power flowing from a deeper source?
How does this teaching deepen your gratitude for satsang?
teachings.reflect: Had you heard the 'actor and roles' idea before? What did you think of it?

teachings.title: A little at a time
parts: The book is honest that understanding Bhagwan Swaminarayan's true greatness is hard. Maharaj himself said that developing conviction in God is more difficult than anything else (Vachanamrut L 18). The book notes that even great sadhus such as Muktanand Swami and Brahmanand Swami took many years to grasp it fully.

So Maharaj taught with compassion, according to each person's capacity. A Gujarati saying captures it: kidine kan, ane hathine man, a grain for the ant and a great measure for the elephant. Give the ant the elephant's share and it is crushed. Maharaj spoke to each audience at the level they could receive, and led them forward gently.

Once Brahmanand Swami wept because they could not openly sing of Maharaj's supremacy everywhere. Maharaj told him to sing in a way that would help countless souls towards liberation. Your own understanding is allowed to unfold in the same patient way. Depth grows through steady contact, not by forcing it all at once.
teachings.quote: people developed conviction in his supremacy gradually over many years
teachings.take: Take in one small teaching today, and let that be enough for now.
reflects: Which part of satsang do you feel you are still slowly understanding?
How does it feel to know great sadhus took years too?
What is your 'grain for the ant' this week?
Where do you put pressure on yourself to understand everything at once?
What has become clearer to you over the last year?
How could you be gentler with your own pace of growth?
Who has explained things to you at just the right level?
What question would you like to carry patiently for a while?
How does Maharaj's compassion in teaching change how you see him?
What small step of understanding would you like to take next?
teachings.reflect: Which part of satsang do you feel you are still slowly understanding?

teachings.title: A lineage without end
parts: Bhagwan Swaminarayan returned to Akshardham in 1830. So how can he still be manifest, present in a form we can meet? The Vachanamrut answers: when God is not personally on earth, one should seek the refuge of the Sant who has realised God, because liberation is attained through him too (V 10).

Maharaj taught that he dwells in Aksharbrahman more fully than in anyone or anything else (G I 41). Yogiji Maharaj explained it with an image: there were many gopis, but Radha was the foremost. In the same way, Maharaj resides completely in the Gunatit Satpurush, the guru who is Aksharbrahman in human form.

In a 1997 letter, Pramukh Swami Maharaj wrote that a queen has as much power as the king, and so Maharaj manifests through Aksharbrahman. The book traces the living succession from Gunatitanand Swami to Bhagatji Maharaj, Shastriji Maharaj, Yogiji Maharaj and Pramukh Swami Maharaj. As Yogiji Maharaj said, it never ends. God is still reachable, in person. Today, that living guru is Mahant Swami Maharaj.
teachings.quote: there is never an end to his lineage
teachings.take: Look at a photo of the guru today and remember Maharaj is present through him.
reflects: What does it mean to you that God is still reachable in person?
Which guru in the succession do you feel most connected to, and why?
How does Yogiji Maharaj's image of Radha among the gopis help you?
When have you felt Maharaj's presence through the guru?
What would you like to ask the guru if you had a moment with him?
How can you take the guru's refuge in a practical way this week?
What story of a guru in this lineage do you love most?
How does an unbroken lineage give you hope for the future?
Who first introduced you to the guru?
What one teaching of the guru would you like to live more fully?
teachings.reflect: What does it mean to you that God is still reachable in person?

teachings.title: Learning from the master
parts: To become a doctor you learn from a professor of medicine; to become an engineer, from a professor of engineering. The book uses this everyday example to explain a central teaching: to become brahmarup, taking on the qualities of Aksharbrahman, we need to associate with Aksharbrahman himself, present on earth as the Gunatit guru.

Maharaj also compared Aksharbrahman to the sun (Vachanamrut G II 42). Once the sun rises, every direction becomes clear. In the same way, through the guru we come to understand Parabrahman as he truly is. The Mundaka Upanishad says one who knows Brahman becomes brahmarup, and Maharaj said that close association passes Brahman's virtues to the jiva (G II 31).

Gunatitanand Swami gave great hope here. He said that if one finds such a sadhu and does as he says, flaws that would have taken countless lifetimes to remove can be overcome now. Association means closeness in thought, word and action: listening to him, following his guidance and keeping him in mind through the day.
teachings.quote: imperfections that would have taken tens of millions of births to overcome are overcome today
teachings.take: Read or listen to a few words from the guru today and act on one of them.
reflects: Who has been a real teacher in your life, and what did you learn from them?
What does associating with the guru look like for you day to day?
Which of your habits would you most like the guru's help with?
How does the image of the sun rising help you understand the guru's role?
What guidance of the guru have you already followed, and what happened?
How does it feel to know change can happen faster than you expect?
Which is easiest for you: thought, word or action? Which is hardest?
What is one instruction of the guru you could act on this week?
How could you keep the guru in mind during your job search?
What quality of the guru would you most like to learn?
teachings.reflect: Who has been a real teacher in your life, and what did you learn from them?

teachings.title: Swami and Narayan
parts: On 31 December 1801, on the fourteenth day after his guru Ramanand Swami passed away, Bhagwan Swaminarayan gave his devotees a new mantra at Faneni village: 'Swaminarayan'. At that time he was known by other names, such as Sahajanand Swami and Narayanmuni. If he only wanted to be worshipped, he could have used one of those. So why this word?

Just as Radha-Krishna and Sita-Ram join God's name with his foremost devotee, 'Swaminarayan' joins Swami, meaning Gunatitanand Swami (Aksharbrahman), with Narayan, meaning Maharaj himself (Parabrahman). Pramukh Swami Maharaj explained that it means devotee with God: we offer true worship to Narayan by taking on the virtues of the ideal devotee, Swami.

Bhagatji Maharaj once asked the young Shastriji Maharaj whether he truly understood 'Swaminarayan'. Shastriji Maharaj replied that he firmly believed Maharaj was supreme God. Bhagatji Maharaj said that was faith in Narayan alone; full understanding also meant knowing Gunatitanand Swami to be Akshar. Every time you chant the mantra, you repeat the whole theology in one word.
teachings.quote: Swami with Narayan, that is, Bhakta with Bhagwan.
teachings.take: Chant 'Swaminarayan' slowly five times, thinking of Swami on the first half and Narayan on the second.
reflects: Did you know the story of where the mahamantra was first given?
What does 'devotee with God' mean to you?
Which of Gunatitanand Swami's virtues would you most like to imbibe?
How might chanting feel different now you know its full meaning?
How would you answer Bhagatji Maharaj's question yourself?
When does chanting 'Swaminarayan' help you most?
Which other pairs, like Radha-Krishna, help you understand this?
What does it teach you that God chose to be named alongside His devotee?
Who in your family taught you to chant, and what do you remember?
How could you bring the mantra into one ordinary moment today?
teachings.reflect: Did you know the story of where the mahamantra was first given?

teachings.title: A mandir for the murti
parts: Once, after hearing five Vachanamruts read aloud twice, Gunatitanand Swami concluded that becoming brahmarup is essential for everyone, whoever they are. Then he turned to a devotee with a picture. If you have a murti but no mandir, where will you install it? First prepare a mandir, and then God will stay (Swamini Vato 3.13).

Our hearts are that mandir. To become brahmarup means to take on the qualities of Aksharbrahman: pure, steady and free from maya's pull. The Shikshapatri asks us to see our true self as brahmarup and to offer devotion to God with that understanding (verse 116). Swami's point is that such a heart becomes a fitting home for Purushottam.

A mandir is built stone by stone, and it takes time. Each kind choice, each moment of patience, each sincere prayer and each piece of seva is another stone laid. Some days you may lay only one, and that still counts. Nothing is wasted, and the One who will live there values every stone.
teachings.quote: You have a murti, but without a mandir where will you install it?
teachings.take: Choose one quality to 'build' today, such as patience in one conversation.
reflects: If your heart were a mandir, which part feels most complete?
Which 'stone' would you like to lay this week?
What does a fitting home for God look like to you?
Which quality of Aksharbrahman inspires you most?
What helps you feel steady inside?
Which small kindness today could be a stone in your mandir?
How does this picture change the way you see everyday effort?
Who helps you build, and how?
What would you like to clear out to make more room for God?
How could you remember this image during a frustrating moment?
teachings.reflect: If your heart were a mandir, which part feels most complete?

teachings.title: The greatest one serves
parts: Aksharbrahman is vast beyond imagining. Maharaj said countless universes float like tiny atoms in each pore of Akshar (Vachanamrut G II 42). He explained with mountains: Girnar looks small beside Mount Meru, and Meru looks small beside Mount Lokalok. The universes do not actually shrink; Akshar is simply that immense.

Yet the book describes one of Akshar's forms as God's eternal servant in Akshardham: a personal, divine form forever engaged in humble devotion and service to Parabrahman (G I 21). Aksharbrahman is also the abode where God lives, the all-pervading consciousness that supports everything, and the guru on earth. It is one reality working in four ways.

The most exalted being after God chooses the role of servant. That turns ordinary ideas of greatness upside down. It also shows what devotion looks like at its highest: not grandness or recognition, but loving service. Every small seva you offer, even one nobody sees, is a step in the same direction as Akshar.
teachings.quote: In its other form, that Akshar remains in the service of Purushottam Narayan.
teachings.ch: Ch. 10, "Aksharbrahman: Attributes", p. 143; Ch. 11, "Aksharbrahman: Forms and Functions", pp. 145-148
teachings.take: Do one quiet act of service today that nobody needs to notice.
reflects: What does greatness usually mean in the world around you?
How does Akshar's choice to serve change that picture?
Which of Akshar's four forms had you not heard of before?
What seva do you find most joyful?
Who do you know who is great but humble?
How could you serve someone quietly this week?
What does the mountain comparison help you imagine?
Where might humility help you in a job interview or at work?
What gets in the way of serving with a light heart?
How does it feel to walk in the same direction as Akshar?
teachings.reflect: What does greatness usually mean in the world around you?

teachings.title: Eighteen quilts
parts: In Vartal, Bhagwan Swaminarayan asked Gunatitanand Swami to serve the sadhus who were ill. Swami washed their quilts. Some healthy sadhus noticed his willingness and handed him their quilts as well. One day, having washed eighteen of them, he met Maharaj near the Hanuman gate and became lost in his darshan.

Back in the assembly, Maharaj said that this sadhu had placed the quilts on his own shoulders, and asked for them to be brought in. The sick sadhus collected theirs; the healthy ones were too embarrassed to come forward. Then Maharaj asked Brahmanand Swami what he knew of this sadhu. Brahmanand Swami praised his bhajans, his seva, his renunciation and his faith.

Maharaj said that was not all. Swami beheld Maharaj's murti within him while awake, dreaming and in deep sleep, and many would one day follow him. Maharaj felt Swami's seva as a weight on his own shoulders, and saw what others missed: the inner greatness of Akshar hidden in humble service.
teachings.quote: That sadhu has burdened the quilts upon my shoulders.
teachings.take: Do one task for someone who cannot repay you, and trust that Maharaj notices.
reflects: What moves you most in this story?
Why do you think Maharaj felt the quilts on his own shoulders?
When has your quiet effort gone unnoticed by people?
How does it feel to know Maharaj notices unseen seva?
What do you think the healthy sadhus learned that day?
How can you serve without keeping score?
What inner quality of someone you know do others tend to miss?
What would it be like to hold Maharaj in mind while doing a chore?
Where might you need to say no kindly, so your seva stays joyful?
Which detail of this story would you share with a friend?
teachings.reflect: What moves you most in this story?

teachings.title: Covered, never spoiled
parts: The book describes the jiva, your true self, in beautiful terms drawn from the Vachanamrut and Shikshapatri: eternal, conscious and blissful by nature, pure, radiant, ageless and indivisible. Nothing can pierce it and time cannot age it. It belongs to no caste or community, and it is described as an embodiment of happiness and knowledge.

Why, then, do we not feel this? The book explains that since time without beginning, the jiva has been covered by maya's ignorance, which it compares to darkness hiding what is really there. This bondage is real, and it takes God and the guru to lift it. But the book makes a striking point: this covering cannot put a single flaw into the jiva's essentially pure form.

Darkness hides a room; it does not damage it. The book says that through association with the Gunatit guru, the covering is removed, and the jiva comes to experience the knowledge and bliss that were always its own. Whatever you are going through, what you truly are has never been spoiled, and it is still his.
teachings.quote: it is unable to bring about any defects in their essentially pure form
teachings.take: In one heavy moment today, remind yourself: what I truly am is still pure and still His.
reflects: Which description of the jiva surprised you most?
How does it feel to hear your true self has never been spoiled?
What do you sometimes believe about yourself that this teaching gently questions?
When have you glimpsed something peaceful and bright within you?
What helps lift the covering a little for you?
How could you speak to yourself more kindly today, knowing this?
Who reminds you of your goodness when you forget it?
What would change if you treated yourself as God's pure creation?
Which of your qualities do you think shines through even on hard days?
What would you like to thank God for about who you are?
teachings.reflect: Which description of the jiva surprised you most?

teachings.title: Made with compassion
parts: Why does the universe exist at all? The book explains that Parabrahman is complete and content in himself, so he gains nothing by creating. He creates out of compassion, to give souls bound by maya the opportunity to become free (Vachanamrut K 1, P 1). The book adds that he shows no partiality or cruelty in how the world works.

Even the great cosmic cycles carry kindness. The book notes that God dissolves the universe for the souls' benefit too: to let jivas, tired from countless births and deaths, rest (K 1). And when he creates again, it is so that they can have another chance to meet him and be freed. Nothing in the cycle is careless or cruel.

Maharaj also taught that the world is not an illusion. Souls, maya and the universe are real (G I 39, 42). So your life, your efforts and your relationships are real, and the world they happen in was made with souls like you in mind. This human life is not an accident; it is an opportunity given with love.
teachings.quote: Creation is borne out of Parabrahman’s compassion
teachings.take: Notice one beautiful thing in the world today and thank God for making it.
reflects: How does it feel to know the world was made out of compassion?
What in your life feels like an opportunity given with love?
Where do you see kindness built into the world around you?
What does it mean to you that your life and efforts are real?
Which relationship in your life are you most grateful for?
How could you use today's opportunity in a small way?
What beautiful thing did you notice this week?
How does the idea of rest for tired souls speak to you?
What would you like to say to God about the world He made?
How might this teaching change the way you see an ordinary morning?
teachings.reflect: How does it feel to know the world was made out of compassion?

teachings.title: Glow-worms and stars
parts: Between God and us in the book's map are the ishwars: immensely powerful beings, such as the Brahma, Vishnu and Shiv of each universe, who help in its creation, sustenance and dissolution. The book says the difference between an ishwar and a jiva is like that between a glow-worm and a star: far greater power and knowledge, and a lifespan as long as the universe.

Yet ishwars are still bound by maya, just as jivas are. All their power depends on Parabrahman, and before Aksharbrahman and Parabrahman they are powerless. For their own liberation, the book explains, even ishwars must take birth as humans on earth and associate with Brahman and Parabrahman, becoming brahmarup (Vachanamrut G II 31).

Pause on that. Beings far greater than us need exactly what you already have: a human birth and the chance to associate with the guru and worship Maharaj. However small you may feel on some days, the opportunity in your hands is one that even the stars must come to earth to receive.
teachings.quote: as distinct as that between glow-worms and the stars
teachings.take: Today, thank Maharaj once for this human birth and the satsang in it.
reflects: Had you heard of the ishwar category before?
How does it feel that even powerful beings need what you already have?
When do you feel small, and how might this teaching speak to that?
What part of your satsang life do you most take for granted?
How could you make more of this opportunity this week?
Which image here stays with you: the glow-worm or the star?
What does 'bound by maya' mean to you in plain words?
Who helped you find satsang in this life?
What would you like to do with this human birth?
How could you express gratitude for satsang in one action today?
teachings.reflect: Had you heard of the ishwar category before?

teachings.title: Freedom while living
parts: Swaminarayan theology speaks of two kinds of liberation. Videha mukti is liberation after this life, when the soul reaches Akshardham. Jivan mukti is liberation while still living: becoming brahmarup and experiencing God's presence and bliss here and now. Maharaj speaks of this living state in the Vachanamrut (S 9, G III 7).

The book explains that such a devotee still meets the results of past karma, but is not shaken by them. They understand that whatever comes is by the will of their beloved God, and that nothing can trouble them without that will. Within themselves they see the manifest form of God, and they live with a steady, even mind in every situation (L 10, G II 1).

The book also defines liberation not only as freedom from suffering but as joy: becoming brahmarup and experiencing God's own bliss. That is the direction satsang points in. It is not just a distant future reward; through the guru's association, that freedom can begin in this life, little by little, one steady moment at a time.
teachings.quote: Everywhere, always, and in all circumstances, he remains in a state of equanimity
teachings.ch: Ch. 15, "Mukti Mimansa: Deep Reflection on Liberation", pp. 199-202
teachings.take: In one tense moment today, pause and remember: this too is within His will.
reflects: Had you thought of liberation as something that can begin now?
What would a steadier mind look like for you this week?
Which situations shake you most easily?
How might remembering God's will soften one of them?
When have you felt a moment of real inner freedom?
What does joy, not just relief, mean to you spiritually?
Who do you know who seems steady in all circumstances?
What small practice helps you feel God within you?
What would 'little by little' look like for you this month?
What would you like to be free of, and what would you like to be free for?
teachings.reflect: Had you thought of liberation as something that can begin now?

teachings.title: Human actions, divine eyes
parts: When Bhagwan Swaminarayan lived on earth, he slept, spoke, walked and travelled like anyone else. The book explains that God often conceals his divinity when he takes a human form, out of compassion, so that people can come close, serve him and offer devotion (Vachanamrut P 7). Yet his form on earth is exactly as divine as his form in Akshardham (G III 31).

The same is true of the Gunatit guru. Gunatitanand Swami taught that true bliss in worship comes when God's human-seeming actions and his divine actions are seen as equally divine (Swamini Vato 5.101). He compared the two ways of seeing to the moon: seeing human flaws makes one's progress fade like the new moon, while seeing divinity makes it grow (5.392).

This is a way of looking, practised over time. When the guru says something that surprises you, or one of Maharaj's leelas (divine actions) seems ordinary, the invitation is to look again with trusting eyes. The book says this understanding helps a devotee rise above maya, and brings real joy into worship.
teachings.quote: true bliss in worshipping God is attained
teachings.ch: Ch. 7, p. 109; Ch. 8, "Parabrahman: Absolutely Divine", pp. 115-120
teachings.take: Recall one ordinary-seeming moment from the guru's life and look for the divinity in it.
reflects: Which ordinary action of Maharaj do you love hearing about?
Why do you think God hides His divinity out of compassion?
When has the guru surprised you, and how did you respond?
What helps you look with trusting eyes?
Which prasang of the guru felt ordinary at first but meaningful later?
How does the moon comparison help you?
What doubt would you like to see with divine eyes instead?
How could this way of seeing bring you more joy in darshan?
Who in your family models this kind of seeing?
What would you like to ask Maharaj about this teaching?
teachings.reflect: Which ordinary action of Maharaj do you love hearing about?

teachings.title: The demons within
parts: Earlier avatars came for particular tasks, often to defeat demons. In old manuscripts and in a letter to his paramhansas and devotees, Bhagwan Swaminarayan explained his own purpose differently: he came to make souls brahmarup and grant them ultimate liberation, and to destroy the ignorance that comes from maya. That, he said, was his sole purpose.

Once, to test his followers, Maharaj pointed out that he had not killed any demons, so why did they call him God? The sadhus answered that the demons of old had themselves fallen to lust, anger and greed. Maharaj had destroyed those very forces inside people, which is greater still. Nishkulanand Swami recorded this answer in the Bhakta Chintamani, and Maharaj was very pleased.

The book notes that through his association, countless men and women, householders and sadhus alike, experienced the bliss of atma and Paramatma while still living. That work continues. Satsang is not only about avoiding what is wrong; it is about Maharaj gently freeing you from what weighs on you from within.
teachings.quote: my incarnation is to make the jivas brahmarup and grant them ultimate liberation
teachings.take: Name one small inner habit, like irritability, and hand it to Maharaj in prayer today.
reflects: What do you think of the sadhus' answer to Maharaj's test?
Why might inner demons be harder to defeat than outer ones?
Which inner habit would you most like Maharaj's help with?
How does it feel that Maharaj's purpose is your freedom?
When have you noticed an old habit loosening its hold?
What helps you ask for help rather than fight alone?
Which story of someone transformed by Maharaj inspires you?
How might you be patient with yourself while habits change?
What does 'freedom from within' mean to you?
What would you like Maharaj to free you for this year?
teachings.reflect: What do you think of the sadhus' answer to Maharaj's test?

teachings.title: The bliss in one pore
parts: Bhagwan Swaminarayan described Parabrahman as the source of infinite, eternal bliss. In Vachanamrut Sarangpur 1 he said he would give up all the pleasures of countless universes for a single second of God's darshan. Gather every joy from every universe, he said, and it would not equal a millionth of the bliss present in one pore of God.

The book adds more: God's is the most blissful form (G III 28), he is the reservoir of every kind of bliss (G III 39), and every joy we seek through the senses exists in him at once (G II 1). This is not a demand to reject happiness. It tells us where happiness finally comes from.

On flat or grey days it can feel as if joy has dried up. This teaching says the source never runs dry, even when we cannot feel it. Every moment of genuine peace in darshan, kirtan or prayer is a drop from that ocean. The ocean is still there, and there is always more.
teachings.quote: for just one second’s darshan of that God
teachings.take: Spend one minute in darshan today simply enjoying Maharaj, asking for nothing.
reflects: When have you felt a moment of real joy in darshan or kirtan?
What does it mean to you that joy has a source that never runs dry?
Which kirtan lifts your mood most?
What small joy did you notice this week?
How could you make room for one minute of simple darshan today?
What would it be like to ask Maharaj for nothing, just to enjoy Him?
Where else do you look for happiness, and how does that compare?
How might this teaching help on a flat day?
Who helps you feel joy in satsang?
What would you say to Maharaj about the bliss you hope to feel?
teachings.reflect: When have you felt a moment of real joy in darshan or kirtan?

teachings.title: Nothing is lacking
parts: In Vachanamrut Gadhada II 14, Bhagwan Swaminarayan says something surprising. A person who truly understands the nature and greatness of God, even with only a modest intellect, should be regarded as highly intelligent. A person without that understanding, however clever in worldly matters, should be seen as lacking real intelligence.

Gunatitanand Swami said the same in his own words: one who has resolute conviction in God's form has completed every endeavour and has nothing more left to do (Swamini Vato 1.123). Maharaj also said that if someone has firm faith in God, a small shortcoming that still remains is nothing to worry about (G II 13).

The world measures people by exams, CVs and job titles. Satsang uses a different scale. Your worth in God's eyes rests on your faith in him and understanding of his greatness, which no interview can take away. That does not make effort pointless, but it puts it in its proper place.
teachings.quote: should still be regarded as possessing much intellect
teachings.take: Before any task that feels like a test today, remember your real worth is already safe with Him.
reflects: What measures do you usually use to judge yourself?
How does satsang's scale feel different from the world's?
Which small shortcoming do you worry about more than you need to?
When have you felt 'not clever enough', and what would Maharaj say?
What does real intelligence mean to you now?
How could this teaching steady you before an interview?
Who do you know who is wise in faith, whatever their qualifications?
What effort feels worthwhile to you, even if results are slow?
How can you keep effort in its proper place this week?
What would you like to remind yourself of on a hard day?
teachings.reflect: What measures do you usually use to judge yourself?

teachings.title: The only guardian
parts: In Vachanamrut Vartal 5, Bhagwan Swaminarayan describes what it means to truly take refuge in God. Such a devotee, even if facing pain as vast as the dissolution of the universe, would not look to anyone else as their protector. God alone is their guardian, and God alone is the one they call on.

He goes on: whatever happiness this devotee wants, they seek it from God; they see no one else as the source of joy, and they live by God's wishes. Maharaj calls such a person a staunch devotee. Gunatitanand Swami added that one who understands God's glory stays happy whatever difficulties or ill health arise (Swamini Vato 1.4).

Taking refuge does not mean you will never struggle. It means that when you do, you know where to turn. And since God is the all-doer, the help that comes through doctors, family and friends is also his help. You can accept it gladly while remembering the One working through it all.
teachings.quote: would not believe anyone to be his guardian against such misery except God
teachings.take: When you feel overwhelmed, say 'You are my guardian, Maharaj', then take one small next step.
reflects: Where do you turn first when things feel too much?
What does taking refuge in Maharaj look like for you in practice?
Which person has been God's help to you recently?
How does it feel to call Maharaj your guardian?
What small next step could you take today, trusting Him?
When have you felt protected during a hard time?
What help are you finding hard to accept, and why?
How could you thank God for the people He works through?
What would you like to hand over to your guardian tonight?
What words would you use to ask Maharaj for strength?
teachings.reflect: Where do you turn first when things feel too much?

teachings.title: The poet-saints of Maharaj
parts: In the early years, scholars in Jamnagar mocked Bhagwan Swaminarayan's sadhus. When humble saints like Atmanand Swami could only say that they obeyed their guru, they were laughed at as unlettered villagers. Maharaj did not argue back. Instead he asked every sadhu to study Sanskrit and philosophy, and to develop music, poetry, singing and the arts until each gift was polished.

Even Muktanand Swami, already in his fifties, sat with younger sadhus to learn Sanskrit from the beginning. Out of this effort came an extraordinary circle of poets. Muktanand Swami could sing, play many instruments and compose. Premanand Swami composed over 14,000 songs and sang so beautifully he could make an afternoon feel like dawn. Nishkulanand Swami, a skilled carpenter, wrote 23 books and over 2,000 songs.

When the poet Dulaa Kaag recited Brahmanand Swami's compositions, tears flowed from his eyes. Years later the sadhus returned to the same courtyard in Jamnagar and, led by Nityanand Swami, answered the same scholars so well that they bowed. The kirtans we sing today were born from patient learning offered to God.
teachings.quote: Until today we thought that sadhus could only sing village rhymes
teachings.take: Pick one kirtan by Premanand, Brahmanand or Nishkulanand Swami and learn what one line means.
reflects: Which kirtan do you love most, and do you know who wrote it?
How might you have felt being laughed at like those early sadhus?
Maharaj answered mockery with learning. What could you quietly learn this month?
Muktanand Swami started Sanskrit in his fifties. What feels 'too late' for you to begin?
Which of your gifts would you like to polish and offer to God?
What does it feel like when a kirtan moves you to tears?
Who in your life has helped you grow a talent?
What small daily practice could turn into something beautiful over years?
Which line from a kirtan has stayed with you, and why?
How could singing be part of your seva this week?
teachings.reflect: Which kirtan do you love most, and do you know who wrote it?

teachings.title: To the beat of bhajan
parts: A doctor's son once rang from New Jersey to ask what Pramukh Swami Maharaj was doing. The answer came back simply: bhajan, of course, what else is there to do? In Mumbai in 1995, children ran upstairs and found him singing. When dinner finished early one evening, he asked what was next, and answered himself: bhajan. Even five spare minutes became singing with Dharmacharan Swami.

Yogiji Maharaj used to tell of a cotton merchant so full of his trade that he asked for 'cotton' to drink when he meant water. Whatever fills the heart spills out naturally. For Swamishri it was bhajan, remembering and singing to God, and it ran through calls, letters, meetings and walks like a fish living in water.

Asked about his hobby, he said bhajan. In his passport, under occupation, he wrote that his work was to do bhajan and inspire others to do it. For him, bhajan was the answer to every problem. The essay says his whole life kept one rhythm: the steady beat of devotion.
teachings.quote: Swamishri breathes to the beat of bhajan.
teachings.take: When you have five spare minutes today, hum one line of a bhajan instead of scrolling.
reflects: What fills your mind most naturally when you are idle?
If someone asked your 'hobby' today, what would you honestly say?
Where could five spare minutes of bhajan fit into your day?
Which bhajan do you find yourself humming without thinking?
What does 'like a fish in water' mean to you in devotion?
How do you feel after singing, compared with before?
Who could you sing with this week?
What would you write under 'occupation' if it described your heart?
When a problem feels heavy, could a bhajan help you face it?
What one rhythm would you like your days to keep?
teachings.reflect: What fills your mind most naturally when you are idle?

teachings.title: Narsinh Mehta's song of empathy
parts: Narsinh Mehta (1414 to 1481) is one of Gujarat's best-loved bhakta-poets. He was born near Junagadh and, as a child, could barely speak. He lost his parents early and was raised by his grandmother. Tradition says an ascetic at a Shiv temple blessed him and asked him to chant 'Radhe Krishna', and his speech returned.

His devotion was not always welcome at home, and he later left to worship on his own. He sang freely, even in the neighbourhoods of the poorest people, which angered the orthodox of his community. His reply came as a song: a true Vaishnav, a beloved of God, is one who feels other people's pain as his own.

When King Ra'Mandalik tested him by locking a garland inside a temple, Narsinh sang through the night, and the story says the garland came to rest around his neck. He left around 740 bhajans. Bhagwan Swaminarayan often asked his own poet-sadhus to sing Narsinh's songs and told devotees to take their feeling to heart.
teachings.quote: He is called a Vaishnav (Hari's beloved) who understands other people's misery
teachings.ch: Sadhu Mukundcharandas, 2005 (from Rishis, Mystics and Heroes of India, Vol. I)
teachings.take: Listen once to 'Vaishnav jan to' today and notice one person whose pain you could ease.
reflects: Narsinh struggled to speak as a child. Where has your voice felt blocked?
Who do you know who truly understands other people's pain?
When did someone last feel your pain as if it were their own?
Where might God be asking you to sing, even if others disapprove?
What does being 'Hari's beloved' mean to you?
Which of Narsinh Mehta's bhajans do you already know?
Why do you think Bhagwan Swaminarayan loved these songs?
How could you show empathy to someone who is struggling this week?
What would you sing through a long night of testing?
Which line of a bhajan has comforted you in a hard time?
teachings.reflect: Narsinh struggled to speak as a child. Where has your voice felt blocked?

teachings.title: Mirabai's refuge in Giridhar
parts: Mirabai was a Rajput princess of the sixteenth century. At three, her grandfather Dudaji helped her receive a small murti of Krishna, which stayed with her for life. When she was seven, watching a wedding procession, her mother told her that Kanha would be her bridegroom. The child took it to heart, and her whole life became a love song to him.

Married into the royal family of Chitor, she faced years of hostility for her devotion. She chose Raidas, a humble leather worker, as her guru, which shocked the court. She answered with bhajans, saying she welcomed their disapproval if it meant staying close to her Lord. She sang to him by many names: Giridhar, Murlidhar, Ghanshyam, Ranchod.

In Vrindavan, a great saint refused to meet her because of a vow. Mira replied that in Vrindavan there was only one man, Krishna, and everyone else was a gopi. He received her. One of her kirtans says the fruit of satsang may taste bitter at first, but becomes as sweet as mango. Tradition says that at the end she merged with her Lord inside the Dwarkadhish temple.
teachings.quote: Mira has taken refuge in Giridhar and shall ever remain at his lotus feet.
teachings.take: Say one of God's names slowly three times today, the way Mira called to Giridhar.
reflects: What small thing from childhood has stayed with you as a link to God?
Mira faced disapproval for her devotion. Have you ever felt that?
Which name of God feels closest to your heart?
What does 'refuge' mean to you on a hard day?
Mira chose a humble guru. What does humility look like in your satsang?
When has satsang felt bitter at first and sweet later?
What would you say in a bhajan if you wrote one tonight?
How can you stay gentle with people who do not understand your faith?
Which of Mirabai's bhajans do you know or would like to learn?
Where do you feel most at home with God?
teachings.reflect: What small thing from childhood has stayed with you as a link to God?

teachings.title: Raidas, the singing cobbler
parts: Raidas was born near Kashi in 1377 into a family of cobblers and became a disciple of Swami Ramanand, alongside Kabir. When his father sent him away for his devotion, he built a small hut outside town. There he mended shoes and sang bhajans all day, worshipping a small murti. In one song he tells the Lord that He is the sandalwood and Raidas is only the water it scents.

A jealous man complained to the king that a cobbler should not worship. At the palace, learned men were asked to call the murti into their laps with mantras, and could not. Raidas simply sang, asking how someone as unsteady as him could offer devotion, and the story says the murti came to rest in his lap.

A sadhu once offered him a philosopher's stone that turned iron into gold. Raidas declined it, and left it untouched on a shelf. Queens and later Mirabai accepted him as their guru. He sang that his birth, deeds and talent were all low, yet the Lord had lifted him up. Honest work and a singing heart were enough.
teachings.quote: I do not want this maya.
teachings.ch: Enlightening Essays, 2005 (from Rishis, Mystics and Heroes of India, Vol. I)
teachings.take: While doing an ordinary task today, quietly sing or chant, as Raidas did at his work.
reflects: Raidas sang while he worked. What task could you pair with a bhajan?
When have you felt 'not good enough' to offer devotion?
What does it mean to you that God lifted a humble cobbler so high?
What 'philosopher's stone' tempts you away from what matters?
Who do you know who does ordinary work with extraordinary devotion?
How do you respond when someone looks down on you?
What would you like your daily work to be filled with?
Raidas called himself water and God the sandalwood. What image would you use?
What does contentment look like in your life right now?
Who could you encourage who feels overlooked?
teachings.reflect: Raidas sang while he worked. What task could you pair with a bhajan?

teachings.title: Gauribai and the missing crown
parts: Gauribai was born in 1759 in Giripur, Gujarat, into a community where everyone could read. Widowed as a small child, she did not despair. She said Bhagwan was her Lord and she had dedicated her life to Him. She stayed with her parents, worshipped, studied scripture and began composing bhajans of her own.

Her reputation grew until the local Raja built a mandir in her honour, where pilgrims, sadhus and scholars came to hear her. Later she travelled to Gokul, Vrindavan, Kashi and Puri. In Jaipur a queen offered her five hundred gold coins; she gave them away. The king then tested her by locking a richly adorned murti in his private shrine and asking her to describe it.

After prayer, Gauribai described every ornament, and added that only one thing was wrong: the crown was missing from the head. The king was astonished and asked forgiveness. She left behind thousands of bhajans, mostly in Gujarati. Her life shows how a woman's quiet, steady devotion could become song that still carries others to God.
teachings.quote: Bhagwan is my Lord and I have dedicated my life to Him.
teachings.ch: Sadhu Mukundcharandas, 2005 (from Rishis, Mystics and Heroes of India, Vol. I)
teachings.take: Write one line of your own prayer or bhajan in a notebook today, however simple.
reflects: Gauribai turned a painful start into dedication. What has shaped your path?
What would you write in a single line of your own bhajan?
Who is a woman of devotion who inspires you?
What does it mean to dedicate a life to God in everyday terms?
Gauribai gave away the gold coins. What is easy or hard for you to let go of?
How does it feel to know God sees what is hidden, like the missing crown?
Where do you go to study or learn about satsang?
What gift could you offer back to God this week?
Which bhajan by a woman saint-poet do you know?
How can you keep your devotion steady when life changes around you?
teachings.reflect: Gauribai turned a painful start into dedication. What has shaped your path?

teachings.title: Holi colours, Fuldol swing
parts: Holi falls on the full moon of Fagun and welcomes spring. Its name is linked to an ancient offering of newly harvested grain to Agni, the fire deity. Several stories gather around it. The best known is of young Prahlad, whose father Hiranyakashipu tried to harm him for his devotion to Vishnu. His aunt Holika sat with him in the fire, yet Prahlad came out safe.

The essay reads this symbolically: maya, the pull away from God, was burnt up by Prahlad's steady devotion. So the true Holi is burning our own unhelpful instincts, and letting ourselves be 'coloured' by God's colour. The day is also celebrated as the birthday of Nar-Narayan Dev. Holi, then, is less about the bonfire outside and more about the change inside.

The next day is Fuldol, the flower swing. It recalls the Yadavs seating Krishna and Arjun on a swing of flowers. When we act to please God, it is as if we pull the swing closer to us. Bhagwan Swaminarayan celebrated Fuldol at Sarangpur and Vartal, and a prayer Nishkulanand Swami versified in the Bhaktachintamani is still sung. At Sarangpur, coloured water is still sprayed during the celebrations.
